sections.heading: The scientific investigation, and the line a tutor does not cross
paragraphs: The investigation carries about a fifth of the SEHS grade and nearly all of the anxiety. It is the one assessment in this subject that involves other human beings: a student measuring heart-rate recovery or reaction time needs willing participants, informed consent, a controlled protocol and a plan for what happens when somebody drops out in week three. Most of the damage we are asked to repair was done at the design stage, weeks before any data existed.

The boundary on help here is set by IB academic-honesty rules and it is not negotiable. The student chooses the question, designs the protocol, collects every measurement, performs the analysis and writes the document. A tutor asks hard questions about scope, confirms a method is repeatable and ethical, teaches the statistics, points at a criterion the student has not yet addressed, and marks a practice version so the gap is visible. A provider offering to supply a finished investigation is offering your child an expulsion risk.

Two practical Abu Dhabi points. Participants are easier to recruit than students think if the protocol is short and does not require maximal exertion, and school sports squads are an obvious and legitimate source once the teacher has agreed. Heat is the second: outdoor protocols designed in November behave differently in April, and a method that depends on a run outside is a method that can fail. We plan around both at the design stage rather than discovering them in the evaluation.
bullets: Design is where the hours pay back; repair work after data collection rarely does
Consent, control and participant safety belong in the plan, not the write-up
Short, repeatable protocols recruit participants more easily than demanding ones

sections.heading: Why a SEHS specialist costs what it costs in Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: The specialist band quoted in this market, roughly AED 200 to AED 450 an hour, is a scarcity price rather than a difficulty price. Three things create the scarcity. SEHS runs in a limited number of Abu Dhabi schools, usually as a single class; the teachers who know it are employed full time by those schools; and the subject is frequently taught by a Biology specialist covering it, which is workable in a classroom and less useful when a parent wants targeted investigation review.

Abu Dhabi adds a regulatory layer. Press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff describes teachers being barred from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, with staff tutoring outside school hours expected to hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. Verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on it. Either way, the person who knows your child's course best is unavailable to you privately.

That is the arithmetic behind online matching, and it is not a sales line. Insisting on someone who can drive to Al Raha by 7.30pm narrows the choice to people who live nearby and are free then. Accepting a live video session widens it to everyone who has taught the current guide. In a subject this thinly staffed in the emirate, that is the difference between a specialist and the nearest available science teacher.

sections.heading: What changes the number on an Abu Dhabi SEHS quote
paragraphs: Two families can be quoted AED 220 and AED 420 for the same subject in the same week, and almost all of the gap is explicable. The largest factor is timing: an autumn slot is a scheduling decision and an April slot is an auction. The second is inclusions. Marking takes a tutor roughly as long as teaching, so a provider returning a marked paper and a written note each week has built that into the figure, and one quoting AED 150 with nothing attached has not.

The third is the component. An hour of content teaching is ordinary work. An hour spent on an investigation that is late involves reading, marking and a difficult conversation about what can no longer be changed, which is why review work is sold as a block rather than by the hour. Level moves the total but not the rate: Higher Level needs more hours, not dearer ones.

The table below is the version worth having before you ring round. It names each driver, what it does to the figure in practice, why it exists, and what a parent can actually do about it. The last column is the useful one: several of these are within your control if you act in October rather than March. One driver parents often miss entirely is cover. A single independent tutor who falls ill in the fortnight before a coursework deadline leaves nobody behind them, and the cost of that gap does not appear in any hourly rate until it happens, which is why we would rather state the cover arrangement in the quote than be asked about it in April.

sections.heading: Sessions, training schedules and the Abu Dhabi calendar
paragraphs: SEHS students are, more often than in any other subject we tutor, students who train. That changes scheduling from an administrative question into the main one. A swimmer with early-morning pool sessions cannot take an 8.30pm slot twice a week and still function at school; a footballer training at a club three evenings a week has two usable evenings and one of them is already homework. The honest planning conversation happens before the first session, not after two cancellations.

The Abu Dhabi year adds its own shape. Ramadan commonly moves sessions to after Iftar, which we plan into the term rather than handling week by week. School examination weeks are better paused than pushed through. The competitive sport calendar has its own peaks, and race and event weekends on Yas Island make Friday scheduling unreliable for families on that side of the city. None of this is unusual; it simply needs to be in the diary from October.

The table sets out the slot patterns that actually work, by student type, with the trade-off each one carries. It is the conversation we have on the phone, written down. Families who pick a pattern and hold it lose fewer sessions across a term than families who book flexibly and reschedule, which matters more than it sounds: a missed session in DP2 is rarely recovered, it is simply gone. The other reason to fix a pattern early is that specialist tutors in this subject hold a small number of slots, and a family who reschedules repeatedly eventually loses the slot to a family who does not.

sections.heading: Is the tutor permitted to teach privately in the UAE?
paragraphs: This is a question any parent can ask and should. Private tutoring in the country is regulated by permit. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through MoHRE, and is granted free of charge for two years. MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time, with applications made through its smart app, website and e-services system. Anybody quoting you a permit fee has invented it.

Eligibility is wider than most parents expect. It includes teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No schedule of amounts has been published, so a specific penalty figure circulating online is unverified and this page will not repeat one.

One distinction matters in practice: an operation with premises and staff in the emirate is a different legal entity from an individual tutor and needs its own permit from the relevant authority. An individual teaching online from home does not become a training institute. And to be plain about ourselves, IB Gram is not approved, endorsed or certified by ADEK, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE, the IB or any examination board. Any provider claiming such status about themselves should be asked for the permit number, and a provider who cannot produce one has told you something useful.

sections.heading: SEHS, university routes and UAE equivalency
paragraphs: The question behind most SEHS enquiries from Abu Dhabi families is whether the subject closes doors. It depends entirely on the destination, and it should be checked against the published entry requirements of the specific universities on the list rather than against a reputation. Many sports science, physiotherapy and exercise physiology degrees accept it directly and welcome it. Medicine and dentistry routes generally expect Biology and Chemistry, and a student taking SEHS instead of Biology should know that before Year 12 rather than during Year 13.

UAE certificate equivalency is a separate process and belongs to the Ministry of Education, not to a tutoring provider. For the British track, the published requirement is five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. For the American track, English proficiency is evidenced by a score of 5 in IELTS academic, 61 in TOEFL iBT or 450 in the SAT reading and writing section, and mathematics by at least 450 in SAT Math.

No IB points threshold for equivalency has been verified for this project, so none is published here. Check the current requirement on moe.gov.ae or with the attestation authority directly, and treat any agency that quotes you a specific IB figure with scepticism until they show the source. Nobody needs tutoring in order to obtain equivalency; it is an administrative process about certificates, and framing it as urgent is a sales tactic rather than a fact.

sections.heading: Online, in-home or group: what the premium buys in this city
paragraphs: In-home tutoring is a real market in Abu Dhabi and families who want it should know what they are paying for. Published in-home rates run from roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour, against about AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified subject tutor working online. The difference is not teaching quality. It is the drive from wherever the tutor lives to wherever you live, at the hour the traffic is worst, plus the student they cannot teach while in the car.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, and saying so on the page is better than letting a family find out after a deposit. Home visits are a service we provide only in India. For UAE families every session is one-to-one over live video, in Gulf Standard Time, with the student's own work shared on screen and marked copies returned afterwards. For a subject taught through graphs, past questions and a coursework document, very little is added by physical presence.

Group classes at a tuition centre are the third option and are genuinely cheaper per student. They suit revision of shared content and are close to useless for an investigation, because the one thing your child needs looked at is the one thing nobody in the room shares. School-run support sessions are the fourth and cost nothing extra, but offer no choice of teacher. Each of these is the right answer for some families; we would rather set them out than pretend there is only one.

whyPoints.description: Half our Abu Dhabi SEHS students train seriously. Slots are built around pool sessions, club evenings and fixture weekends, with a standing alternative for the weeks fixtures move, because a missed DP2 session is rarely recovered.

whyPoints.description: Nobody can guarantee a mark, and a provider who offers to is telling you about their sales process rather than your child. What an hour a week offers is a marked paper, a named weakness and a specific thing to practise before the next one.

faqs.question: What is the going rate for a SEHS tutor working with Abu Dhabi students?
faqs.answer: Specialist Diploma rates quoted in this market run from roughly AED 200 to AED 450 an hour, read in October 2026. Below about AED 150 you are generally buying a non-specialist working from a textbook rather than the current subject guide. Above AED 500 you are paying a reputation premium that should be evidenced. The figure reflects scarcity rather than difficulty: few teachers in the emirate have taught this subject. IB Gram quotes per 60 minutes in writing after a free trial lesson, with marking and a written session note inside the rate.

faqs.question: Is Sports Exercise and Health Science really a lighter group 4 choice?
faqs.answer: The content load is lighter than Biology and the mathematics is lighter than Physics, so the reputation is not baseless. The assessment style is not light at all. Students must read data from exercise physiology precisely, apply it to named sporting situations and obey the command term, and they must design and report an investigation involving human participants. In our Abu Dhabi caseload the first marked paper is where the surprise usually lands. It is a different kind of demanding rather than an easier subject.

faqs.question: How do I find out whether my child's Abu Dhabi school is running SEHS this year?
faqs.answer: Ask the IB coordinator directly, and ask two things: whether the subject is running for your child's cohort and at which level. Group 4 option blocks in this emirate depend on numbers, and a subject can appear on the sheet one year and not the next. We do not publish a list of which school teaches what, because such a list goes out of date within a year and a parent relying on it plans around a course their child cannot take. The school is the only reliable source.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help design an investigation that uses other students as participants?
faqs.answer: Yes, within strict limits. A tutor can question whether the research question is narrow enough, confirm the protocol is repeatable, check that consent and participant safety are planned rather than improvised, and teach the statistics the data will need. The student recruits the participants, runs every trial, records every measurement, performs the analysis and writes the document. Nothing is handed back rewritten. School squads are a legitimate participant source once the teacher has agreed, and short protocols recruit far more easily than demanding ones.

faqs.question: How many hours does an Abu Dhabi SEHS student usually need before the May session?
faqs.answer: Two patterns are common in our caseload. A weekly hour through DP1 term two and DP2 comes to roughly fifty hours across the two years and costs less per mark gained. A compressed plan is a six to eight hour investigation block plus fifteen to twenty hours of paper technique in the final term. Students starting in February of DP2 use more hours for less movement, because content gaps and coursework pressure arrive together. These are our own observations rather than a published standard.

faqs.question: My daughter trains six mornings a week. Can sessions realistically fit?
faqs.answer: They can, but the plan has to be built around the training rather than squeezed beside it. The pattern that works for early-morning swimmers and runners is one weekend morning session plus one weekday evening, with work set between them so the week is not empty. Late twice-weekly slots after evening training look fine on paper and produce tired, unproductive hours. We would rather agree a realistic two-slot pattern in October and hold it than book four slots and lose two every month.

faqs.question: Does my child need Biology alongside SEHS for a medical degree?
faqs.answer: Most medicine and dentistry routes expect Biology and Chemistry, and SEHS is generally not accepted in place of Biology for them. Many sports science, physiotherapy and exercise physiology degrees accept it directly and value it. The decision should be made against the published entry requirements of the specific universities on your child's list, checked on their own admissions pages, and ideally before the Year 12 option sheet is signed rather than during Year 13 when changing a subject is difficult.

faqs.question: Why is a SEHS tutor harder to find in Abu Dhabi than a Biology tutor?
faqs.answer: Supply. The subject runs in a limited number of schools in the emirate, usually as one class in a year group, so very few teachers have taught it. Those who have are mostly employed full time. Press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules describes school staff being barred from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, which removes the obvious candidate. Verify that wording against ADEK's own policy document. The practical result is a short local list and a waiting period, which is what the rate reflects.

faqs.question: Do the data-based questions actually carry recoverable marks?
faqs.answer: They are the most recoverable marks in the subject. The common failure is describing a trend without quoting a value, a unit or a comparison, which scores a fraction of what the student knows. The fix is mechanical: quote the evidence, then interpret it, then link it to the physiology. A term of marked practice usually moves this measurably, and it is the first thing we drill with a student whose content knowledge is sound but whose paper marks are not. No tutor can promise a grade, but this is technique rather than talent.

faqs.question: Should we pay for an investigation block or a term of weekly sessions?
faqs.answer: If the investigation is unchosen or newly started, the block is the better purchase: hours spent narrowing a question in November remove several hours of repair in March. If the content itself is shaky, weekly sessions first and the block later works out cheaper, because an investigation written on weak physiology needs both fixed anyway. Families who buy the block after data collection has finished are paying specialist rates for damage limitation, which is the most expensive version of this subject.

faqs.question: Does the heat in Abu Dhabi affect what protocols are workable?
faqs.answer: It affects outdoor protocols significantly. A method designed in November that requires participants to run outside behaves differently in March and April, and data collected across both is not comparable. We raise this at the design stage, because the alternative is discovering it in the evaluation section, where it becomes a limitation the student has to explain rather than a problem they avoided. Indoor protocols using school facilities are usually the safer design for a student collecting data into spring.

faqs.question: Can one tutor take both SEHS and Biology for the same student?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and it can save time rather than only money. Respiration, circulation and homeostasis appear in both syllabuses with different emphasis, and one tutor can stop a student answering a SEHS question with molecular Biology detail the command term never asked for. The rate is per hour rather than per subject, so two subjects in one hour means less time on each. In DP2, with an investigation deadline approaching, separate hours are usually the better arrangement.

faqs.question: What does an in-home SEHS tutor in Abu Dhabi charge?
faqs.answer: Published in-home rates in this market run from about AED 180 to AED 500 an hour, against roughly AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified subject tutor working online. The premium pays for travel, fuel and the hour the tutor cannot teach anyone else. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; home visits are a service we provide only in India. For a subject taught through graphs, marked past questions and a coursework document, presence in the room adds very little to the teaching.

faqs.question: What happens if no SEHS specialist is free in the slot we need?
faqs.answer: We tell you, rather than offering a general science tutor at a specialist rate. In practice there are three honest options: take a different slot that a specialist does have, start with a Biology specialist for the physiology content while waiting for a SEHS slot to open, or wait. Which one makes sense depends on how close the deadline is and whether the problem is content or technique. Availability in March and April is the tightest of the year, which is the argument for holding a slot in the autumn.

faqs.question: How should I compare two SEHS tutoring quotes from Abu Dhabi providers?
faqs.answer: Convert both into cost per marked, documented hour. Ask whether the rate is per 60 minutes or per lesson and how long a lesson runs; whether marking of set work is included and whether feedback is written; what happens in May if the tutor becomes unavailable; and which subject guide and cohort the tutor last taught. Then request the cancellation rule in writing. Most of the apparent gap in this market closes once both quotes answer the same five questions.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-sports-exercise-and-heal.closingHeading: Book the slot before the calendar decides for you
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-sports-exercise-and-heal.closingBody: If you are looking for an IB DP Sports Exercise and Health Science tutor in Abu Dhabi, the useful first step is a free trial lesson with the tutor who would actually teach. Your child brings their own marked work, and afterwards you get a written view of where the marks are going, how many hours a realistic plan needs, and a rate per 60 minutes with inclusions stated. Sessions run one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, scheduled around training and fixtures. Specialist slots in this subject are scarce in the emirate and April availability is the tightest of the year, so autumn is the sensible time to hold one.

intro.heading: A subject with no paper still produces evidence every fortnight
paragraphs: Families who buy tutoring for Maths or Chemistry get a feedback loop for free. There are past papers, there are marks out of a known total, and a parent can see a score move from 41 to 55 without understanding a single question. Diploma Theatre offers none of that. There is no examination paper at either level. Everything is submitted coursework, marked once, months after the work is done, by someone the family will never meet. So the ordinary way of checking whether tutoring is worth the money simply does not apply, and families either stop asking or stop paying.

There is a better answer, and it is specific rather than reassuring. Theatre produces hard artefacts continuously: notebook pages, a source list, a presentation script, a rehearsal log, a video of a solo piece, a project report. Each of those exists or does not exist on a given date, and each is readable by a parent who has never studied the subject. Progress in Theatre is the accumulation of those artefacts against the requirements of the task, and it is measurable fortnight by fortnight without any judgement about artistic quality.

That measurement is the organising idea of this page. Rather than describing the four assessed tasks as a syllabus tour, the sections below set out what should exist by when, what a weak version of each artefact looks like next to a strong one, and which symptoms mean the work has stalled rather than slowed. A parent who can read those signals can tell within three weeks whether a tutoring block is earning its fee, which is considerably sooner than a Diploma result arrives.

Abu Dhabi matters to this because of cohort size. ADEK licenses and inspects the private schools in the emirate and publishes its own inspection ratings, and Theatre runs in a minority of the schools offering the Diploma here. A cohort of three or four is normal. Where a department is thin or a teacher is covering Theatre alongside another subject, the internal checkpoints that would catch a stalled notebook in a larger school are not there, and the first time anybody notices is close to the internal deadline. That gap is what most families in this emirate are actually buying somebody to fill.

IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Theatre support here is one-to-one over live video, which suits the written half of this subject well and does not pretend to cover the other half. Nobody directs a performance over a screen, and this page does not claim otherwise. What a screen does well is read a notebook page beside the production image it refers to, scrub a rehearsal recording, and track a source list week on week. The published market band for IB specialist tutoring runs at AED 200-450 an hour.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theatre-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Where a Theatre student came from predicts what their evidence trail looks like in the first term. The routes below are the ones that feed Diploma Theatre in Abu Dhabi schools, with the habit each one builds and the one it leaves missing.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme Arts
programmes.description: MYP arts assessment runs on four criteria and a process journal kept alongside the practical work. The journal is the single most useful inheritance for Diploma Theatre, because the director's notebook is a process document and students who have kept one before understand that the record is the assessed object rather than a souvenir of the project.
programmes.countryNote: Only a minority of Abu Dhabi Diploma students arrive through MYP, and in Theatre the proportion is lower still. Where a student does, the first fortnight of support usually confirms the journal habit transferred and then moves straight to the subject's own vocabulary, which shortens the block considerably.

programmes.name: IGCSE Drama
programmes.description: IGCSE Drama combines a written paper on a set text and extracts with practical coursework in devised and scripted performance. It builds performance confidence and the ability to write about a text in rehearsal terms. What it does not build is independent research into an unfamiliar theatre tradition, which is where the Diploma's research presentation lives.
programmes.countryNote: Most Diploma Theatre students in this emirate come through IGCSE Drama, because the British-curriculum cohort here is large. Their evidence trail in term one is usually strong on rehearsal notes and empty on sources, which is exactly the diagnosis the first session tends to reach.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Theatre
programmes.description: Theatre is taken at Standard or Higher Level. Both levels submit a director's notebook on a published play text the student has not staged, a research presentation on a theatre tradition and its conventions, and a collaborative project with a report on an original piece created by the group. Higher Level adds the solo theatre piece, in which a student presents work based on an aspect of theatre theory, with a video and a written report.
programmes.countryNote: Theatre runs in a minority of the Abu Dhabi schools offering the Diploma, often with one teacher and a cohort small enough to fit around a table. The internal checkpoints that catch a stalled notebook in a bigger cohort are frequently absent, and the first warning in this emirate tends to arrive very close to the internal deadline.

programmes.name: Extended Essay in Theatre
programmes.description: A 4,000-word research essay on a theatre question, supervised in school and marked externally. The reliable failure is a question that invites a plot summary of a favourite production. Support is process coaching and feedback on drafts the student has produced, with the essay remaining entirely their own work.
programmes.countryNote: A number of Abu Dhabi students write an Extended Essay in Theatre without taking the subject, usually after a school production. Those students need the analytical vocabulary before the question, and their evidence trail in term one is a reading list rather than a draft.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theatre-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Theatre students rarely book one subject alone. The subjects below are the ones that most often appear in the same request from Abu Dhabi families, with what each assesses and the point where a Theatre student typically needs help.

subjects.name: Theatre
subjects.description: Director's notebook, research presentation and collaborative project report at both levels, plus the solo theatre piece at Higher Level. Marks leak to notebooks that describe a play rather than propose a staging, presentations that summarise a tradition without conventions, and reports with no individual evidence in them.

subjects.name: English A: Literature
subjects.description: Two papers on literary works plus an individual oral and, at Higher Level, an essay. Theatre students often take it and then find that writing about a play as a reader and writing about it as a director are different skills that look alike on the page.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Unseen non-literary analysis in Paper 1, comparative literary essay in Paper 2, plus an individual oral. The overlap with Theatre is the move from a specific textual detail to a claim about effect, which both courses reward and neither teaches overnight.

subjects.name: Film
subjects.description: Textual analysis, comparative study and film portfolio, with a collaborative project at Higher Level. Taking Theatre and Film together means two documentation-heavy courses with internal deadlines in the same weeks, so sequencing beats extra teaching in either.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Comparative study, process portfolio and exhibition, all submitted. Students carrying Theatre and Visual Arts have four separate process documents running at once, which is a scheduling problem long before it is a subject problem.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Papers plus a historical investigation with a source-evaluation section. That section is the closest relative in the Diploma to the research presentation's sourcing demands, and students who do one well usually improve at the other.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Arabic is mandatory in UAE private schools alongside the licensed international curriculum, with placement set by a student's background. For a Theatre student it is usually the subject competing for the evenings on either side of a rehearsal week.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: An exhibition of three objects with commentaries plus a prescribed-title essay. Theatre students reach for arts-and-knowledge prompts and write about taste. The repair is structural: one claim, one counterclaim and one real example per paragraph.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Papers across approaches and options plus an internal investigation. It pairs naturally with Theatre for students interested in audience and performance, and the investigation's method sections are where those students most often need help.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: The cultural district puts live performance within reach, which matters because the research presentation and the notebook are both stronger when a student has watched something staged rather than only read about it. Schools here generally have a drama space with a timetable attached to it.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Tower living means rehearsal happens at school or not at all, so a student's practical evidence is bounded by the department's room booking. Students here benefit most from support scheduled around the days they actually have access to a space.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Villa communities with space at home for solo rehearsal and a long evening drive to anything on the island. For a Higher Level solo piece that combination is helpful: the rehearsal can happen at home and only the recording needs a room.

regions.note: Older island neighbourhoods close to long-established schools, several with proper performance spaces built in rather than retrofitted. Students here usually have rehearsal access and need help with the written half of the subject.

sections.heading: The four artefacts a Theatre parent can actually read
paragraphs: A parent does not need to know anything about theatre to audit progress in this subject. Each assessed task produces a physical thing that either exists on a given date or does not, and the existence question is the one worth asking. Asking whether the sessions are going well invites a yes. Asking to see the current notebook page count, the source list, or the rehearsal log invites an answer that can be checked.

The director's notebook is a document about staging a published play the student has not performed in, built up over months and bounded by a page limit. The research presentation is a recorded piece on a theatre tradition, its conventions and a moment from it, with a time limit. The collaborative project produces a group piece and an individual report. At Higher Level the solo theatre piece produces a short performance video and a written report on an aspect of theory. Each of those has a limit, and the limit is part of the task.

Confirm every page count, running time and word limit with your child's teacher and against the current subject guide. No figure in this project has been verified against ibo.org, which blocks automated requests, and the IB revises components. The table below is there so a family knows which object to ask for at which point, not so that it becomes the authority. The column that matters most for monitoring is the last one, because an artefact that should exist by a date and does not is the earliest reliable warning available.
bullets: Ask for the artefact, not for an opinion about the sessions
Each task has a stated limit that is part of the assessment

sections.heading: A fortnight of Theatre support, and what should exist at the end of it
paragraphs: The most useful promise a Theatre tutor can make is not about a grade. It is that every fortnight ends with something readable that did not exist at the start of it. That standard is easy to state, easy to check, and uncomfortable for anyone selling open-ended sessions, which is precisely why it is worth holding to.

The shape of a block follows the artefact. Early fortnights produce decisions: the play chosen for the notebook, the tradition chosen for the presentation, the theory aspect chosen for the solo piece. Middle fortnights produce volume: notebook pages, a source list that has grown, a draft script with a running time attached. Late fortnights produce cuts, because almost everything in this subject arrives over its limit and the student's instinct is to cut the justification rather than the description.

The table below sets out a worked first block, with what the parent should be able to see and the signal that something has gone wrong. A fortnight that produces a conversation and no artefact is not a disaster once. Two in a row means the work has stalled, and the honest response is to change the diagnosis rather than to buy more sessions. Reviewing on the artefact rather than on the atmosphere is also what keeps a block bounded, which is the single biggest saving available in this subject. A block agreed as eight weeks and four artefacts ends in eight weeks. A block agreed as support with Theatre ends when somebody finally asks what it achieved.

sections.heading: Reading a director's notebook draft the way a moderator would
paragraphs: The notebook is the task where the gap between a student's effort and their mark is widest, and the reason is almost always the same. The student has produced a thoughtful, well-presented document about a play. The task asks for a document about staging a play, which is a different object. One describes meaning; the other proposes a decision, in a specific space, for a specific audience, and justifies it.

A useful session is a line-by-line read on a shared screen. The question asked of every page is whether a reader could build something from it. A note saying the scene is tense is not actionable. A note saying the scene plays with the audience on three sides, the actors never closer than two metres, and a single practical lamp carried by the younger character is a decision somebody could realise, and it can then be justified from the text. Students learn this distinction quickly once it is pointed at, and the second half of a notebook usually improves sharply once they have.

Length is the other recurring problem, and it runs in both directions. A notebook far under the limit at the end of DP1 is a stall. A notebook far over it three weeks before the internal deadline is a cutting job, and the pages students volunteer to lose are the ones carrying their reasoning. The table below contrasts weak and strong versions of the moves the notebook is actually marked on, which is faster to absorb than any amount of description.

sections.heading: The research presentation: progress counted in sources, not slides
paragraphs: The research presentation asks a student to investigate a theatre tradition they have not studied, identify its conventions, and show one moment from it in practice, inside a time limit. It is the task where Abu Dhabi students arrive with the least transferable experience, because IGCSE Drama and school productions both work inside a broadly western theatrical frame and the presentation deliberately pushes outside it.

Progress here has an unusually clean measure: the source list. A presentation with four substantial sources is further along than one with a polished slide deck and two web pages, regardless of which looks more finished. So the artefact to ask for in the early fortnights is the reading list, not the presentation. Students resist this because slides feel like progress and reading does not, and the resistance is itself diagnostic.

There is a trap specific to this task that is worth naming. A student picks a tradition, reads about its history, and presents the history. The task wants conventions, which are the rules about how performance works in that tradition, and then a demonstration of one. History is background; conventions are the content. Sessions on this task spend most of their time converting what a student has read into a short list of conventions they could actually show, and then cutting the running time, which always overruns on the first attempt because the history has not yet been thrown away. The honest version of this task is a short list of conventions, one demonstrated moment, and a great deal of interesting reading that never makes it into the recording.
bullets: Ask for the source list before asking about the slides
Conventions are the assessed content; history is background
The demonstration has to be of one named moment, not a survey
First drafts overrun because the research has not yet been cut

sections.heading: The collaborative project: evidencing your own work inside a group
paragraphs: The collaborative project asks a group to create an original piece from a starting point, and each student to submit their own report on the process and their own contribution. That structure produces a predictable injustice. A student who worked hardest but logged nothing writes a vague report. A student who logged everything writes a specific one. The grade follows the report.

So the evidence discipline in this task is a log, kept from the first rehearsal, with dates. What was proposed, by whom, what was tried, what was kept, what was abandoned and why. Ten minutes after each rehearsal is enough. Students who do this have a report that writes itself from their own material in DP2. Students who do not are trying to recall a rehearsal from eight months earlier, and the result reads as general because it is.

A tutor's role here is narrow and worth being clear about. Nobody outside the group directs the piece, attends the rehearsals or arbitrates its disagreements, and this page does not suggest otherwise. What outside support does is install the log in the first fortnight, read it periodically to check it is specific rather than decorative, and later help the student structure a report from their own entries. The report is written by the student, every word of it. The table sets out what a usable log entry looks like beside the version students usually produce, and the gap between the two columns is roughly the gap between a specific report and a general one.

sections.heading: The Higher Level solo piece: progress from theory aspect to recording
paragraphs: The solo theatre piece is the Higher Level task, and it stalls earlier and more often than any other in this subject. The stall is not performance nerves and it is not rehearsal time. It is the theory. A student has to choose an aspect of theatre theory, explore it in a short solo performance, and write a report about that exploration, and the whole task collapses if the aspect chosen is too broad to be explored in a few minutes.

The progress markers are therefore sequential and easy to monitor. First, a named aspect, narrow enough to state in one sentence. Second, a performance idea that tests the aspect rather than illustrating it. Third, a rehearsal recording. Fourth, a report drafted inside its word limit. A student who has been working for two months and cannot say the aspect in one sentence has not started, however much rehearsal has happened, and that is a diagnosis a parent can reach without knowing any theory.

Abu Dhabi students carry an additional constraint here: a cohort of one. Where a student is the only Higher Level Theatre candidate in their year, nobody in the building has scoped this task before, and the teacher is often meeting it for the first time alongside. That is the single most common reason families in this emirate buy support for one task only. The table below sorts real aspect choices into workable and unworkable, because the difference is faster to see than to describe.

sections.heading: When progress stalls: five diagnoses and what each one costs
paragraphs: A stalled Theatre student looks the same from the outside whatever the cause, which is why families often buy the wrong intervention. More sessions fix one of the five causes below. The other four need something different, and in two cases the right answer is to stop paying for tutoring and talk to the school instead.

The commonest cause is a decision that has not been made. A notebook cannot grow until a play is chosen; a presentation cannot be researched until a tradition is; a solo piece cannot be rehearsed until an aspect is named. Students experience the undecided state as being busy, because they are reading and thinking, and the artefact count does not move. That diagnosis is cheap to fix and the fix is a single session that ends with a decision written down.

The costly causes are different in kind. A student with no rehearsal access cannot produce practical evidence, and no amount of online support substitutes for a room. A student whose group has fractured has a collaborative project problem that belongs to the teacher. A student who has lost confidence after a poor piece of feedback needs a different conversation entirely. The table names each one with the signal that distinguishes it, because distinguishing them is most of the value and it takes one honest session rather than a term of sessions. A provider who reaches the same diagnosis for every stalled student is not diagnosing anything.

sections.heading: What a predicted grade in Theatre rests on, and what it does not
paragraphs: Parents in this emirate ask about predicted grades more often in Theatre than in any other arts subject, usually because a university application needs one and nothing about how it was reached is visible. The honest answer is that a predicted grade is the subject teacher's professional judgement, made from the coursework in front of them, and no external tutor produces, influences or validates it.

What the prediction rests on is the state of the artefacts. A student with a notebook at full length, a sourced presentation and a specific contribution log gives a teacher something to predict from. A student whose work is mostly still intended gives them very little, and a cautious prediction in that situation is not unfair. This is the most practical argument for the fortnightly evidence habit: it puts real material in front of the person making the judgement, early.

Two things follow. First, anybody who suggests that tutoring raises a predicted grade is describing something they cannot deliver and should be read with real scepticism. Second, the way to improve a prediction is to improve what the teacher can see, which is the same work as improving the actual submission. There is no separate strategy. A tutor who understands the task can help a student get their material into a readable state sooner, and that is the whole of the honest offer. A family worried about a cautious prediction should ask the teacher what material would change it, then make sure that material exists.
bullets: A predicted grade is the subject teacher's judgement alone

sections.heading: ADEK, the permit, and who you are actually buying from
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE runs on a permit rather than on trust. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, it is granted free of charge for two years, and it covers teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time, applied for through the ministry's app, website and e-services.

Because it costs nothing, a tutor without one is not economising. People offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published, so no amount is quoted here, and figures circulating online could not be verified against a ministry source. For a parent the useful inference is modest: a free, two-day permit that has not been obtained says something about how the arrangement is run.

Abu Dhabi carries a further rule worth knowing in a small-cohort subject. Press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics framework for private and charter school staff describes a prohibition on teachers giving paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, with the permit's code of conduct reported to carry a similar restriction; verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document. In Theatre this matters more than usual, because the teacher who would be tutoring is often the same person marking the coursework and writing the prediction.

process.title: Send the artefact, not a description of it
process.description: Before the free trial lesson, send the actual material: the notebook as it stands, the source list, the contribution log, the rehearsal recording. A description of how the work is going tells a tutor nothing useful. The trial is then spent reading real material against the real requirements. One free trial lesson per student, booked without card details.

process.title: Agree what the first fortnight has to produce
process.description: The first session ends with a written statement of what should exist in two weeks: a decision, a page count, a source list, a draft inside its limit. That statement is the measure the block is judged on afterwards, and agreeing it upfront is what stops a Theatre arrangement drifting for a term.

process.title: Fix the limit before the content
process.description: Page counts, running times and word limits are part of each task, and almost every Theatre draft arrives over its own. Settling the limit in the first fortnight means the student shapes the work to it rather than amputating their reasoning in the final week to make the pages fit.

process.title: Review on the artefact every fortnight
process.description: Each review compares what now exists against what was agreed. Two consecutive fortnights with nothing new means the diagnosis was wrong, and the response is to change it rather than to add sessions. This is the step that keeps a block bounded and is where most of the saving in this subject sits.

process.title: Keep the school in the loop and in charge
process.description: Internal deadlines, rehearsal access, moderation and the predicted grade all belong to the school. Where the stall is a room booking or a fractured group, the right call is to the subject teacher rather than to us. Saying so costs us a booking and is the correct advice.

whyPoints.title: Progress defined as artefacts, not impressions
whyPoints.description: In a subject with no examination paper, the only honest measure is whether readable material exists that did not exist a fortnight ago. Every block here is reviewed on that basis, which is uncomfortable for open-ended arrangements and useful for families trying to decide whether to continue.

whyPoints.title: Requirements read against the actual draft
whyPoints.description: Sessions work line by line through the notebook, the presentation script or the report, checking each against what the task requires rather than against a general sense of quality. Page counts, running times and word limits are treated as part of the task because the assessment treats them that way.

whyPoints.title: A clear boundary on what a tutor produces
whyPoints.description: Teaching, questioning and marking-style feedback on the student's own drafts and recordings. No written pages, no presentation script handed over, no text for a report. The boundary is published here because it is the real differentiator in a search where completed coursework is sold openly.

whyPoints.description: Nobody directs a performance over live video, and this page does not pretend to. Rehearsal, performance and room access stay with the school. What the online format does well is read a page beside the image it refers to and track evidence fortnight by fortnight.

faqs.question: How can I tell whether Theatre tutoring is working when there is no exam paper?
faqs.answer: Ask for the artefact rather than for an opinion. Every fortnight should end with something readable that did not exist before: more notebook pages, a longer source list, dated contribution log entries, a draft inside its limit, a rehearsal recording. Count it. A fortnight that produces a good conversation and no new material is acceptable once. Two in a row means the work has stalled and the diagnosis needs changing, not topping up. That test works whether or not you know anything about theatre, and it gives you an answer within about three weeks.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a Theatre tutor to our home in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Theatre support here is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. This page is deliberate about the limits of that: nobody directs a performance through a screen, and rehearsal, performance and room access stay with the school. What live video does well is read a notebook page beside the production image it refers to, scrub a rehearsal recording, and track an evidence trail fortnight by fortnight.

faqs.question: My child's director's notebook is beautifully written but the teacher says it misses the point. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly because it is a document about a play rather than a document about staging one. A notebook that explains what a scene means is doing literary analysis. The task asks for decisions a reader could actually build: where the audience sits, how far apart the actors stand, which light moves and why, each justified from the text. Students fix this quickly once it is pointed at, and the second half of a notebook usually improves sharply. It is also why the page count alone is a poor measure of progress in this task.

faqs.question: What should I ask to see at the end of the first month of support?
faqs.answer: Three things, and all of them are countable. A written statement of which artefact the block is targeting and what is missing from it. A decision that has been made and recorded, whether that is the play, the tradition or the theory aspect. And a measurable increase in the artefact itself: pages, sources or log entries. If the answer after four weeks is that your child is thinking about options and the sessions are going well, you have bought a conversation rather than progress, and that is worth raising immediately.

faqs.question: Why is the research presentation the component Abu Dhabi students get wrong first?
faqs.answer: Because it deliberately pushes outside the frame they know. IGCSE Drama and school productions both work within a broadly western theatrical tradition, and the presentation asks for an unfamiliar one, its conventions, and a demonstration of one moment from it. Students research the history of the tradition and present that instead, which is background rather than content. The early measure of progress here is the source list, not the slide deck, and a student with four substantial sources is further along than one with twenty polished slides and two web pages.

faqs.question: How do we keep a contribution log for the collaborative project without it becoming a chore?
faqs.answer: Ten minutes after each rehearsal, four lines, with the date. What was proposed and by whom, what was tried, what was kept, what was dropped and why. That is enough. The entries that matter most are the ideas that failed, because a report built from abandoned proposals evidences process far better than one built from successes. Students who do this have a report they can write from their own material. Students who do not are reconstructing a rehearsal from eight months earlier, and the vagueness shows in the grade.

faqs.question: My child is the only Higher Level Theatre student in their year. Does that matter?
faqs.answer: It matters most for the solo piece. Nobody in the building has scoped that task before, the teacher may be meeting it for the first time alongside your child, and there is no older student's work to look at. The practical consequence is that the theory aspect often stays too broad for months, which stalls everything downstream. Three or four hours early in DP2 spent narrowing the aspect to something that can be stated in one sentence and tested in a few minutes of performance is the best-value purchase available in this subject.

faqs.question: How narrow does the solo piece theory aspect have to be?
faqs.answer: Narrow enough to state in one sentence and demonstrate in a few minutes. A practitioner's name is not an aspect, and neither is a whole form, because both invite a history essay rather than an exploration. The interruption of narrative to force judgement works. Weight transfer as a way of showing status works. Direct address as a break in the fiction works. A student who has been rehearsing for two months and still cannot say the aspect in one sentence has not started the task, whatever else has happened in the room.

faqs.question: Can a tutor write the collaborative project report if my child runs out of time?
faqs.answer: No, and anybody offering to is selling something that puts the diploma at risk. The report has to be the student's own, every word. What a tutor can properly do is help the student structure it from their own log entries, question whether a claim is actually evidenced, and give marking-style feedback on a draft the student has produced. That boundary appears on this page because it is the genuine differentiator here: one page ranking for these searches sells completed assessments outright, and the student carries the consequence.

faqs.question: Does tutoring raise a predicted grade in Theatre?
faqs.answer: Not directly, and any provider implying otherwise should be read with real scepticism. A predicted grade is the subject teacher's professional judgement, made from the coursework in front of them, and no external tutor produces, influences or validates it. What does change a prediction is the state of the artefacts: a full notebook, a sourced presentation and a specific contribution log give a teacher something to predict from. Improving what the teacher can see is the same work as improving the submission, so there is no separate strategy to buy.

faqs.question: What does Theatre support cost per hour for an Abu Dhabi family?
faqs.answer: Published market bands put specialist IB tutoring at roughly AED 200-450 an hour and above. Unitors lists IB from AED 200, TutorChase publishes AED 270, and Bestimate's 2026 tutoring cost table puts one-to-one visits at AED 180-350 with specialist work at AED 200-450 and higher. Cheaper online options exist from around AED 33-65 but sit at the university-student end and rarely work at task level in this subject. Those are other providers' published figures as at October 2026, not an IB Gram price list.

faqs.question: Can we book support for one artefact rather than the whole course?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for most Abu Dhabi families it is the better purchase. A block aimed at one artefact has a visible finish line: the notebook reaches its length and its requirements, the presentation gets its sources and lands inside its running time, the report gets structured from the log. Blocks that target the course in general drift for a term because nothing in them can be marked complete. If the work finishes before the sessions do, the block ends early rather than rolling on into something nobody is reviewing.

faqs.question: Our school cannot give my child rehearsal space. Can tutoring fix that?
faqs.answer: No, and it would be dishonest to take the booking on that basis. Practical evidence in this subject needs a room, and no amount of online support substitutes for one. If the written work is progressing and the practical evidence is absent, the problem is access and the conversation belongs with the subject teacher or the head of year. Where rehearsal happens at home, as it often can for a solo piece in a villa community, a recording made there is usually enough, and reviewing that recording on a shared screen works well.

faqs.question: How do Ramadan and school production weeks change a Theatre support plan?
faqs.answer: Both matter more here than in examined subjects. Ramadan shifts school hours and household routines across the UAE, and post-Iftar sessions usually work better than late afternoon ones. School production weeks are the bigger disruption in Theatre specifically, because the department, the space and the students are all committed and no coursework moves at all. Blocks are planned around both, with the heavy written work placed in the quieter fortnights either side rather than scheduled into weeks where nothing can realistically be produced.

faqs.question: Do Theatre tutors working with Abu Dhabi students need a MoHRE permit?
faqs.answer: Individuals providing private tutoring in the UAE need a MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years and covers school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Those tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no figure appears here. The permit is free, so its absence is worth asking about.

faqs.question: What happens if no Theatre specialist is free when we need one?
faqs.answer: You are told before anything is booked. Theatre is one of the thinnest subjects in this market, and Higher Level solo piece supervision is thinner again. Where no UAE-resident specialist covers the task, the match comes from the wider pool of Diploma Theatre tutors working to Gulf Standard Time, most often from India, in the same online format and on the same hourly basis, with the tutor's location stated upfront rather than afterwards. Flexibility on timing widens the choice: a 19:30 slot reaches a materially larger pool than a fixed 17:00 one.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theatre-home-tutor.closingHeading: Send the notebook, the log and the source list
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theatre-home-tutor.closingBody: An IB DP theatre home tutor in Abu Dhabi is worth paying for when the arrangement is measurable. Send the artefact as it actually stands, the school's internal deadline, and which task is the problem, and the free trial lesson will tell you what is missing and roughly how long it will take to fix. Sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, every fortnight ends with something readable, and rehearsal and performance stay with the school. Every page and every word submitted remains your child's own, and nothing on this page promises a grade.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theatre-tutor.tutorsIntro: Theatre tutors on IB Gram are matched by the task in front of your child: a notebook on an unfamiliar play text, a solo piece built on a theorist, a research presentation that has to demonstrate rather than describe, or a collaborative project that has drifted. You see the tutor's subject background before the trial lesson.

intro.heading: Why Theatre is the one Diploma subject where the money does not follow the exam calendar
paragraphs: Most tutoring budgets in Abu Dhabi are shaped the same way. A family spends lightly through DP1, then sharply from January of DP2 as mock papers come back and the May session approaches. Theatre breaks that pattern completely. There is no written paper to revise for, no past-paper archive to drill, and no grade boundary waiting at the end of a two-hour examination. Every mark in DP Theatre comes from work that is written, recorded and uploaded, and those uploads are due well before the examination window the rest of the cohort is worrying about.

The practical consequence for a parent in Khalifa City or on Al Reem Island is that the expensive months are the wrong ones. Spending on Theatre peaks when a director's notebook draft is due and when a solo theatre piece report is being cut down to its word limit. By the time a family is paying for Physics revision in March, the Theatre marks are already fixed and uploaded. Families who budget Theatre like a science subject routinely pay for hours at the point where those hours can no longer change anything.

That timing difference is also why Theatre quotes look strange next to other subjects. A tutor who charges AED 220 an hour for IB Chemistry may quote the same figure for Theatre and then deliver something completely different for it: not worked examples and timed questions, but a read of a 20-page notebook, a viewing of a recorded presentation, and a conversation about whether a chosen theorist can actually be staged by a seventeen-year-old in a school studio. The hour is the same length. What it buys is not comparable.

Abu Dhabi adds a second wrinkle. Theatre is a small-cohort subject. A Diploma school on Saadiyat Island or in Al Raha Gardens may have six or eight Theatre candidates in a year group, and a single teacher covering the whole course alongside MYP Arts. That teacher is capable and usually excellent, but they are not available at 8pm on a Thursday when a report is due on Sunday. Local tutor supply reflects the same arithmetic: there are far fewer Theatre specialists in the emirate than there are Maths tutors, which is exactly why delivery is online and why the pool a family draws from should not be limited to who lives within a twenty-minute drive.

This page is written around the money. It sets out what the Abu Dhabi market charges in AED and who publishes each figure, which of the four Theatre tasks drives the bill, what moves a quote up or down in this emirate specifically, and how the spend is distributed across the two Diploma years. ADEK regulates the private schools your child attends, and the rules that govern who may tutor privately in the UAE are federal. Both are covered below, with sources, because a price with no context is just a number.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theatre-tutor.programmesIntro: Theatre runs across three IB programmes, and the money behaves differently in each. A parent paying for Diploma Theatre support is usually paying for task-shaped feedback; a parent paying at MYP level is usually paying for the writing and reflection habits that make the Diploma tasks cheaper later.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Theatre
programmes.description: Theatre sits in Group 6, the arts. At Standard Level a candidate submits a director's notebook, a research presentation and a collaborative project. Higher Level adds the solo theatre piece, built on an aspect of theatre theory the student chooses and then has to perform and defend. None of it is examined in a hall. All of it is written up, recorded and uploaded against limits published in the subject guide.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi the Diploma Theatre cohort at any one school is usually small, which means a candidate rarely has a classmate working on the same theorist or the same play text. That isolation is the most common reason an Abu Dhabi family reaches for a tutor: not weakness in the subject, but the absence of anyone to argue with about a draft at the point where arguing is what improves it.

programmes.name: MYP Arts, into Diploma Theatre
programmes.description: MYP Arts is assessed on four criteria and rewards process documentation. A student who keeps a usable process journal in MYP 4 and 5 walks into Diploma Theatre already able to evidence a decision, which is most of what the director's notebook asks for. A student who has only ever performed arrives able to act and unable to justify, and the first paid Diploma hours go on a skill that should have been free.
programmes.countryNote: Several Abu Dhabi IB continuum schools run MYP Arts as a carousel across drama, music and visual art, so a student may reach DP1 with one term of drama in three years. Families in Khalifa City and Al Raha Gardens often ask for a short block of MYP 5 sessions for exactly this reason, and it is the cheapest Theatre intervention available.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme and the arts route
programmes.description: A small number of UAE schools offer the Career-related Programme, where a student takes DP courses alongside a career-related study. A CP candidate taking Theatre as a DP course sits the same tasks with the same limits, but carries a different overall workload and a reflective project instead of the full Diploma core. The tutoring question is therefore scheduling rather than content.
programmes.countryNote: CP provision in Abu Dhabi is thin compared with Dubai, so a family exploring it is usually comparing one local option against a Dubai school and a commute. Online delivery removes the tutoring half of that decision: the Theatre support does not change if the school does.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theatre-tutor.subjectsIntro: A Theatre tutor is matched by task, not by a general subject label. These are the pieces of DP Theatre an Abu Dhabi family actually buys hours against, with what each is assessed on and where the hours tend to go.

subjects.name: Solo theatre piece
subjects.description: A piece based on an aspect of theatre theory the candidate selects, performed and written up in a report with a recording. The expensive mistake is choosing a theorist who reads well and cannot be staged in a school studio. Early hours spent testing that choice save a far larger number later.

subjects.name: Director's notebook
subjects.description: A notebook responding to an unfamiliar published play text, submitted within a page limit. Marks are lost by describing staging ideas without justifying them against the text, and by running out of pages before reaching the moments that would have scored.

subjects.name: Research presentation
subjects.description: A recorded presentation on a theatre tradition outside the candidate's own experience, with a source list. It must demonstrate a convention practically, not narrate its history. Presentations that are essentially illustrated lectures are the single most common pattern in weak submissions.

subjects.name: Collaborative project
subjects.description: An original piece created by a group from a starting point, written up individually in a report with a video. The individual report is where marks move, and it is where one student usually ends up documenting a process four students ran unevenly.

subjects.name: Theatre theory and theorists
subjects.description: Brecht, Stanislavski, Boal, Artaud, Lecoq and others appear across all four tasks. A tutor's job is to make one theorist genuinely usable for this student's piece rather than to survey a reading list, which is what most online summaries do.

subjects.name: Play text analysis
subjects.description: Reading a text for staging rather than for meaning: entrances, sightlines, the moment a scene turns, what an audience can physically see from the third row. This is the skill the director's notebook is actually testing and the one most Diploma candidates have never been taught explicitly.

subjects.name: World theatre traditions
subjects.description: Kathakali, Noh, commedia dell'arte, Beijing opera, Ta'ziyeh and others. The research presentation requires one tradition studied properly, including convention, mask or movement vocabulary, and a cited source base that is not three encyclopaedia pages.

subjects.name: Process journals and reflective writing
subjects.description: Every Theatre task is written up, and the writing is marked. Reflective writing that reports what happened scores poorly; writing that explains a decision and its consequence scores. This is teachable in a small number of sessions and is the best value hour in the subject.

subjects.name: Performance skills for assessment
subjects.description: The solo piece and the collaborative project are both recorded. Camera framing, audibility, and keeping the assessed moment inside the recording are practical issues that cost real marks and take minutes to fix if someone raises them before the shoot rather than after.

subjects.name: Theatre alongside the Diploma core
subjects.description: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay compete for the same evenings as a Theatre deadline. An Extended Essay in Theatre is possible and is a different piece of work from the solo piece; keeping the two separate is a planning conversation worth having in DP1.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theatre-tutor.regionsTitle: Theatre families across Abu Dhabi, and what the week looks like
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-theatre-tutor.regionsIntro: Abu Dhabi Diploma families are spread between the island, the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor, and the newer mainland communities. Rehearsal and recording commitments make Theatre scheduling different from other subjects, so the realistic session slot varies by where a family lives and which school the student attends.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Served by international Diploma schools with studio space and arts staffing. Students here usually have rehearsal access and need feedback hours rather than facilities, often late evening after a school production block.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: A dense residential pocket with a short school run and several Diploma cohorts. Sessions commonly land at 5pm or 6pm, and recording work happens at home at weekends because studio bookings are competitive.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Villa communities feeding a cluster of British and American curriculum schools alongside IB provision. Theatre candidates here are frequently the only one in their friendship group taking the subject, which is why remote peer-style discussion matters.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens and Al Raha Beach
regions.note: A short hop from the airport road and home to an IB continuum intake. Families often book around a sibling's activity schedule, so a fixed weekly Theatre slot is more valuable than a flexible one.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Older island neighbourhoods with established schools and heavy mid-afternoon traffic on the Corniche approach. A 4pm session is rarely realistic; 6.30pm onwards works, and online delivery removes the drive entirely.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and Al Karamah
regions.note: Central mainland districts with a mix of long-standing private schools. Theatre candidates here often combine the Diploma with external performance commitments, so the support has to flex around production weeks.

regions.name: Yas Island and West Yas
regions.note: Newer housing with growing Diploma numbers. Distance from older island schools means some students have a 40-minute commute each way, which makes an evening online slot the only workable one during a term.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Shakhbout City
regions.note: Large mainland communities where families are more price-sensitive and more likely to compare a group option against one-to-one. For Theatre the comparison usually resolves in favour of one-to-one, because the tasks are individual.

schoolClusters.note: The island carries most of Abu Dhabi's long-established Diploma provision, and these are the schools whose Theatre candidates most often have studio access and a dedicated arts teacher. Students we support come from across this cluster; the support is additional to their school course, not a replacement for it.

sections.heading: What an IB DP theatre tutor in Abu Dhabi costs, by tier and format
paragraphs: Market rates for Diploma tutoring in Abu Dhabi run from roughly AED 45 an hour at the budget end to AED 650 at the top, and the spread is explained almost entirely by who is teaching rather than by what subject is being taught. EdFlik publishes rates from AED 45 to AED 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to AED 52, both for online group or entry-level work. Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. TutorChase quotes AED 270. Bestimate's Dubai rate table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to AED 350 and subject specialists at AED 200 to AED 450 and above. BartyED publishes AED 650 for its premium tier. Every one of those figures is the provider's own published number, and none of them is an IB Gram price.

For Theatre specifically, the tier that matters is the third one. A budget tutor can mark an English essay competently and cannot usefully comment on whether a Lecoq-derived movement sequence will read on camera. The qualified-teacher band, AED 150 to AED 300 an hour, is where a genuine Theatre background starts, and the specialist band above it is where a tutor has taken candidates through a solo theatre piece before and knows what a marker does with a report that justifies nothing. Paying the budget rate for Theatre is usually paying twice: once for the hour, and again for the redraft it did not prevent.

Package pricing seen in this market is worth knowing before a quote arrives. Monthly offers of around AED 799 for eight online sessions, and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits, both circulate in the UAE. Bestimate's monthly estimates for one weekly hour run AED 240 to AED 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support. A Theatre family should treat monthly packages with care for one reason: the subject's workload is not monthly. Four sessions in the week a report is due are worth more than eight spread evenly across a quiet term.

Our own position on money is simple. IB Gram does not publish an hourly price on this page, because the figure depends on the tutor matched and the task in front of them. What we do publish is the market, with sources, so a parent can tell whether a quote they have been given is cheap, normal or expensive before they say yes to it.

sections.heading: Four tasks, no examination paper, and what each one does to the bill
paragraphs: Theatre is assessed entirely through submitted work. A Higher Level candidate produces four pieces; a Standard Level candidate produces three. Each carries a published weighting and a published limit on length or duration, and each fails in a predictable way. Understanding which task is in front of your child is the difference between buying the right six hours and the wrong twelve.

The solo theatre piece is Higher Level only and is the heaviest single item at Higher Level. It asks the candidate to take an aspect of theatre theory, create and perform a piece from it, and write a report with a recording. The failure mode is almost never performance quality. It is the choice made in week one: a theorist selected because the summary sounded impressive, which then cannot generate four minutes of stageable material. A tutor's most valuable hour on this task is the first one, before anything is committed.

The director's notebook responds to an unfamiliar published play text inside a page limit, and the research presentation is a recorded presentation on a theatre tradition the candidate has not previously studied, with a source list. Both are marked on justification rather than coverage. A notebook that describes a lighting state scores less than one that explains why that state serves a specific moment in the text. A presentation that narrates the history of a tradition scores less than one that demonstrates a convention and then explains what the demonstration proved. The collaborative project is group-made and individually written up, and the report is where the marks sit, which is why a strong group with a weak writer still scores badly.

Limits are published in the subject guide and the IB revises them between guide editions, so confirm the exact figures for your child's cohort with their Diploma coordinator rather than with any website, including this one. What does not change is the principle: the limit is binding, and running out of pages before reaching the scoring material is one of the most common and most avoidable losses in the subject.
