abu-dhabi/ib-home-tuition.modesIntro: Three household rhythms work over two Diploma years. They differ in frequency and session length rather than in content, and the right one depends on how much of the week is already committed.

modes.title: One long slot a week
modes.description: Ninety minutes, one subject, one fixed evening. The best fit for Mathematics and the sciences, where a topic needs runway and a sixty-minute session spends its first ten minutes recovering context. It is also the most robust rhythm for a busy household, because there is only one appointment to protect each week rather than two.
bullets: 90 minutes weekly at a fixed slot in Gulf Standard Time
Timed assessment every second session
Shared document updated in the session, not afterwards
Survives a busy week better than two shorter appointments

modes.title: Two short slots a week
modes.description: Sixty minutes twice, with two or three days between them. The spacing is the point: a topic taught on Monday and re-tested on Thursday is retained far better than one taught in a single long block. It suits content catch-up and examination preparation, and it needs a household that can genuinely protect two evenings.
bullets: Deliberate two-to-three day gap for spaced retrieval
Better for content gaps than a single longer session
Shorter sessions suit a tired student late in the week
Needs two protected evenings, which not every household has

modes.title: Defined coursework block
modes.description: A short run of sessions attached to a specific internal deadline: an exploration, an investigation, an Extended Essay draft or an oral rehearsal. Finite, quoted as finite, and scheduled against the school's own internal calendar rather than ours. Most valuable in the DP1 to DP2 summer and the first weeks of DP2.
bullets: Scheduled from the school's internal deadline backwards
Drafts annotated against criterion letters, never rewritten
Typically four to eight sessions with a clear end
Best booked before the autumn deadline crush, not during it

sections.heading: Home tuition as a two-year plan rather than a rescue
paragraphs: A Diploma is a two-year commitment with a predictable internal shape, and a tutoring arrangement that ignores that shape ends up doing the same thing in all four phases of it. The pattern is reliable enough to plan against. DP1 is content, with coursework appearing from the second term. The intervening summer is open and almost always wasted. The first term of DP2 is where internal deadlines and mock examinations collide. The second term is examination preparation, where sessions should get shorter and more frequent.

The expensive mistake is starting in the wrong phase. Families overwhelmingly make contact in the first term of DP2, which is the single worst moment to begin: coursework deadlines are fixed, predicted grades are about to be set, and any content gap from DP1 now has to be closed in competition with work that has a date on it. The same support bought a year earlier costs the same money and does roughly twice as much.

The other mistake is a plan that never changes. A weekly ninety-minute session is right for DP1 content work and wrong for the eight weeks before final examinations, when the student needs frequent short sessions built around timed papers. If the arrangement in March of DP2 looks identical to the arrangement in October of DP1, nobody has been planning; they have been renewing. The table below is the shape worth planning against, checked each term against the school's own internal calendar rather than assumed.

Short and frequent, reducing in the last week

sections.heading: The household timetable, and the hour that actually exists
paragraphs: Almost every failed tutoring arrangement in this emirate started with an hour that was never real. A family books 17:00 because it sounds like after school. The school day ends at 15:30, the bus or the car gets home somewhere between 16:00 and 16:35 depending on which side of the bridge you live, the student needs food and twenty minutes of nothing, and a younger sibling needs collecting at 16:45. The 17:00 session begins at 17:12 with a student who has not eaten.

The hour that holds is usually later than families first propose. In the Khalifa City and Shakhbout City catchment, where runs are short, 17:30 works. For households in Al Raha Beach, Al Falah or out towards Al Reef, 19:00 to 19:30 is the slot that survives a term. Where there are sports or co-curricular commitments two or three evenings a week, a weekend morning is frequently the only genuinely protected time, and a ninety-minute Saturday session is better than a Tuesday one that is cancelled every third week.

This is also the clearest practical advantage of video delivery and the one nobody advertises. A visiting tutor's start time is set by their own driving day, which pushes it towards the earliest hour they can manage, which is frequently the worst hour for the student. A video session has no travel constraint at either end, so the slot can be chosen entirely around the student. Picking 19:30 because that is when a sixteen-year-old is actually able to think is not a compromise; it is the whole point.

sections.heading: Ramadan, the UAE calendar and when revision actually happens
paragraphs: Ramadan reorganises an Abu Dhabi household for a month, and a tutoring plan that does not acknowledge it loses four to six sessions and often never restarts. School hours shorten, the working day shifts, and the usable study window moves to after Iftar. Nothing about that is a problem if it is planned in February. It is a serious problem if the first conversation about it happens in the second week.

The practical pattern that works is a later, shorter session: sixty minutes rather than ninety, starting after the meal, with the content chosen for lower cognitive load. Past-paper review and draft annotation work well at that hour. Teaching a genuinely new and difficult topic does not, and attempting it produces a session everyone remembers as unproductive. Where a student is fasting and tired, reducing to one session a week for the month and compressing afterwards is a better decision than pushing through and losing the habit entirely.

The calendar matters beyond Ramadan too. Internal coursework deadlines do not move for it, which is why a plan that pauses for a month in DP2 can put an Extended Essay submission in real difficulty. Nor does the May examination session move. Counting backwards in weeks from the session, rather than forwards from today, is the only way to see whether a month at reduced intensity is affordable. For most DP1 students it is. For a DP2 student in the second term it usually is not, and the honest answer is to shorten the sessions rather than suspend them.

sections.heading: What a household actually needs on the desk
paragraphs: The equipment question gets either ignored or wildly overstated. What a Diploma student needs for a video session is modest, and the single most important item is not the computer. It is a way to show handwritten working as it is produced. For Mathematics and the sciences, where most marks sit in the method rather than the answer, a tutor who can see only the finished line is marking a conclusion instead of teaching a process.

A phone on a ten-dirham stand, angled at the page, solves this completely. A tablet with a stylus solves it more elegantly. Neither needs to be new. What does need attention is the calculator: it must be the model from the school's own permitted list, because teaching keystrokes on a different device introduces a term of small, untraceable errors. Headphones matter in an apartment, and a desk that faces away from a television matters more than any specification on this list.

What is genuinely not required is a second screen, a drawing tablet, a paid subscription or a particular laptop. The table below separates the two categories, because households routinely spend money on the wrong half. Everything in the required column together costs less than a single in-home session at the Abu Dhabi market rate of AED 180 to 500 an hour. The optional column is where households spend first and gain least, usually because a shop assistant was more persuasive than a tutor. One more point belongs here, because it matters more than any item on the list: the desk has to be somewhere the student is not performing for an audience. A dining table with two siblings and a television behind it produces a session that looks perfectly reasonable on the recording and teaches almost nothing, and no equipment on the market compensates for that.

sections.heading: Keeping the timetable alive when the family travels
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi households travel, and they travel at exactly the points in the Diploma calendar when continuity matters most: the DP1 to DP2 summer, the winter break between the DP2 deadline crush and examination preparation, and Eid. A tutoring arrangement that only exists while everyone is in the emirate loses between a quarter and a third of the available year, and loses it in the most valuable weeks.

Because sessions run over live video, the schedule converts rather than stops. A slot fixed at 19:30 Gulf Standard Time becomes 15:30 in London, 21:00 in Karachi and 17:30 in Nairobi, and the arithmetic is worth doing once in advance rather than weekly in a message thread. Where a time difference makes the usual slot impossible, moving to a weekend morning for the duration of the trip is simpler than cancelling and restarting.

Two things make travel survivable in practice. The first is agreeing, before the trip, which sessions will run and which will not, so a gap is a decision rather than a drift. The second is the recording: a session missed for a wedding in Hyderabad is recoverable because the previous three are still available, and the shared document says what was set. Families who handle travel this way keep the DP1 summer, which is the highest-value and least used window in the whole programme. Worth adding: a trip is also an opportunity rather than only an obstacle. Three weeks with no school and no co-curriculars is the easiest time in the year to run two sessions a week instead of one, and a household that shifts to a heavier rhythm while travelling often arrives back in September further ahead than it would have been at home.

sections.heading: Pausing on purpose, and what a pause costs
paragraphs: Not every gap is a failure. There are points in the Diploma where stopping is the right call, and recognising them is part of planning rather than a lapse in it. The week of school mock examinations is one: an extra session the night before produces fatigue rather than marks, and the student's time is better spent on their own revision. The fortnight after final examinations is another. A genuine family event is a third.

What distinguishes a useful pause from a damaging one is whether it has an end date agreed when it starts. A pause with a restart date in the diary costs nothing. A pause described as a few weeks costs most of a term, because the slot gets given away, the habit breaks, and the conversation about restarting keeps being deferred until something goes wrong. The difference is administrative and it decides outcomes.

Cost should be explicit too. Sessions not taken are not charged, there is no retainer for holding a slot, and a slot released for more than three weeks may not still be available on return, which is a real consequence rather than a penalty. Where a pause lands in the second term of DP2 the honest advice is usually to shorten sessions rather than suspend them, because the examination date does not move and the weeks cannot be recovered later. The one pause nobody should take is the quiet one: three missed sessions in a row with no conversation about any of them. That is not a pause, it is the end of the arrangement happening without anyone deciding, and it is worth naming out loud the first time it happens rather than the third.

sections.heading: A minor's data: recordings, forms and what is kept
paragraphs: Household tuition for a sixteen-year-old involves personal data about a child, and the UAE has a statute on this: Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on the Protection of Personal Data. Almost no page in this market mentions it, and every page in this market collects a child's name, school, year group and often their grades through a form. Those two facts sit uncomfortably together, so here is the position in plain terms.

What is collected is what the arrangement needs: the student's first name, year group, subject and level, the school for context, and a parent's contact details. What is not needed is a photograph, a full academic history or a national identity document, and a form asking for those without saying why is asking for too much. Marked scripts and session recordings are held so the student can revise from them and a parent can review them, not for any other purpose, and they can be deleted on request.

Three related points. A privacy link belongs on every page that carries a form, including this one. Recordings are shared with the family rather than published or used as marketing material, and nothing identifiable about a child appears on this site. And the stated purpose has to match the actual use: a form that says it is for matching a tutor should not feed anything else. None of this is onerous, which is why its absence across this market is difficult to excuse.

sections.heading: The federally required subjects sitting alongside the Diploma
paragraphs: An Abu Dhabi Diploma student is not studying six subjects. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations, so those commitments occupy timetabled hours alongside the IB courses. For a household planning evening capacity, that is the difference between the timetable they imagine and the one their child is actually carrying.

The most detailed public articulation of how these subjects are organised comes from Dubai's regulator rather than Abu Dhabi's, and it is worth reading even if your child is in Abu Dhabi, because it shows the shape of the requirement. Published KHDA guidance states that Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of different curriculum expectations and language of instruction.

That guidance also sets out language of instruction in detail: Standard Arabic for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, Arabic as the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students, and the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in Moral, Social and Cultural studies. It adds that instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, and that for mandatory subjects the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is strictly prohibited. That last line is a genuine constraint on how any tutoring in these subjects can be described, and it is why support here is framed as examination technique and language skill rather than alternative content. Confirm your own school's arrangements with the school, since these are Dubai's published requirements.

sections.heading: How tuition reaches an Abu Dhabi household
paragraphs: One-to-one, over live video, at a fixed slot in Gulf Standard Time. The session uses a shared whiteboard, a document camera or phone stand so handwritten working is visible in both directions, and the actual past paper annotated live on screen rather than a retyped version of it. Sessions are recorded and the recording goes to the family. A shared running document holds what was taught and what was set, so nothing depends on a teenager's account of the hour.

IB Gram does not send tutors into households anywhere in the United Arab Emirates. Visiting a student's address is a service we run only in India, and that is not a soft position that bends for a good customer. Where a family's requirement is specifically that an adult is physically present, which is a reasonable requirement for a primary-age child, we are the wrong provider and will say so rather than take the booking.

What the household gains is the size of the pool. For a Diploma subject at Higher Level, the set of specialists who could reach a given Abu Dhabi community by 18:00 is frequently empty, while the set who teach that paper is not. Coverage is disclosed before anything is paid: the common subjects start within a week, Group 2 languages beyond French and Spanish take longer, and Higher Level Further Mathematics, Design Technology and Music are genuinely thin. Where nothing suitable is free you are told so and offered a later slot, a wait, or nothing.

process.title: Count the hours that genuinely exist
process.description: Before choosing subjects, work out how many protected evenings the household actually has once the school run, food, co-curriculars and a younger child's bedtime are counted. In most Abu Dhabi households the honest answer is two. Choosing two subjects and protecting them beats choosing four and losing all of them by November.

process.title: Fix the slot around the student, not the tutor
process.description: Because no travel is involved, the slot can be chosen entirely around when a sixteen-year-old can think. For households on the Al Raha and Al Reef side that is usually 19:00 or later. Picking the hour that holds for a whole term is worth more than picking the hour that sounds like after school.

process.title: Free trial lesson, then a plan across both years
process.description: The trial is a real lesson with the tutor who would teach, booked without card details. What follows is a term-by-term outline for the rest of the Diploma, checked against the school's own internal deadline calendar rather than a generic one, with the coursework blocks placed where they will actually be needed.

process.title: Agree Ramadan, travel and pauses in advance
process.description: Decide in writing what happens during Ramadan, over the summer and across family travel, before any of them arrives. A pause with a restart date in the diary costs nothing. A pause described as a few weeks costs most of a term, because the slot is released and the habit breaks.

process.title: Review each term against the evidence
process.description: At the end of each term the first diagnostic sits beside the most recent one, with the recurring-error count from the log. That comparison decides whether the rhythm changes, the tutor changes, or the arrangement stops. Carrying a plan into a second year without that review is how two years of fees buy one year of progress.

whyPoints.title: Planned across two years, not renewed monthly
whyPoints.description: A term-by-term outline for both Diploma years, placed against the school's own internal deadlines. The shape changes between a DP1 content term and the eight weeks before final examinations, and an arrangement that looks identical in both has not been planned at all.

whyPoints.title: The slot is chosen around the student
whyPoints.description: No travel at either end means the hour can sit at 19:30 because that is when a tired sixteen-year-old in Al Raha Beach can actually think. A visiting tutor's start time is set by their own driving day, which is why in-home sessions cluster at the worst hour of the evening.

whyPoints.title: Ramadan and travel handled before they arrive
whyPoints.description: Post-Iftar sessions, shortened rather than suspended, agreed in February. Converted slots for a month in London or Karachi, agreed in June. Most arrangements in this emirate die in one of those two windows, and both failures are administrative rather than academic.

whyPoints.title: Visible without being intrusive
whyPoints.description: A recording the household can sample, a shared running document showing what was taught and set, marked scripts returned rather than described, and a fortnightly note. That is more information than overhearing a lesson provides, and it is dated and comparable.

whyPoints.title: Honest about a minor's data
whyPoints.description: What is collected is the student's first name, year group, subject, level, school for context and a parent's contact. No photograph and no academic history. Recordings go to the family and nowhere else, and they can be deleted on request. Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 is the reason that sentence belongs on the page.

whyPoints.title: Finite blocks quoted as finite
whyPoints.description: Coursework support, a mid-year arrival catch-up or an oral rehearsal are defined pieces of work with an end. They are quoted that way rather than converted into an open-ended weekly commitment, which is the default behaviour of the agency model and the reason so many families feel unable to stop.

faqs.question: When in the two Diploma years should an Abu Dhabi household start tuition?
faqs.answer: DP1, and ideally its first term. Families overwhelmingly make contact in the first term of DP2, which is the worst available moment: internal coursework deadlines are fixed, mock examinations are about to set predicted grades, and any content gap carried from DP1 now competes with work that has a date attached. The same support bought a year earlier costs the same and achieves considerably more, because there is room to teach something properly rather than to triage. If you are already in DP2, start anyway, but expect the first block to be deadline management rather than teaching.

faqs.question: What time should we actually book, given an Abu Dhabi school run?
faqs.answer: Later than most families first suggest. A school day ending at 15:30 puts a student home between 16:00 and 16:35 depending on which side of the bridge you live, after which they need food and twenty minutes of nothing. In the Khalifa City and Shakhbout City catchment, 17:30 holds. For Al Raha Beach, Al Falah or Al Reef, 19:00 to 19:30 is the slot that survives a full term. Because no tutor is travelling, the hour can be chosen entirely around the student rather than around a driving schedule, which is the single most useful scheduling freedom video delivery gives you.

faqs.question: Through Ramadan, does the weekly Diploma session keep running in this household?
faqs.answer: They shorten and move rather than stopping, and the pattern is agreed before the month starts. Sixty minutes after Iftar rather than ninety before it, with content chosen for lower cognitive load: past-paper review and draft annotation work well at that hour, while teaching a difficult new topic does not. For a DP1 student, dropping to one session a week for the month and compressing afterwards is entirely reasonable. For a DP2 student in the second term it usually is not, because the examination session does not move and those weeks cannot be recovered later.

faqs.question: We spend six weeks abroad every summer. Does the plan survive that?
faqs.answer: It survives if the arithmetic is done in June rather than negotiated weekly in July. A slot fixed at 19:30 Gulf Standard Time becomes 15:30 in London, 21:00 in Karachi and 17:30 in Nairobi. Where the time difference makes the usual hour impossible, moving to a weekend morning for the duration is simpler than cancelling. This matters more than it sounds, because the summer between DP1 and DP2 is the highest-value window in the whole Diploma: six weeks with no teaching, no homework and every internal deadline still in front of the student.

faqs.question: What equipment does our household actually need?
faqs.answer: Less than you would expect, and the most important item is not the computer. For Mathematics and the sciences, where marks sit in the method rather than the answer, the tutor has to see working as it is produced: a phone on a cheap stand pointed at the page does this completely, and a tablet with a stylus does it more elegantly. The calculator must be the model from the school's own permitted list, because keystrokes differ between permitted devices. Headphones matter in an apartment. A second monitor is useful at Higher Level and not required. The whole required list costs less than one in-home session at market rate.

faqs.question: How many subjects can one household realistically support at once?
faqs.answer: Two, in most cases. The constraint is protected evenings rather than money. A Diploma student already has homework, coursework, the service component and, in an Abu Dhabi school, Arabic and the other federally required subjects on the timetable. Adding four weekly tutoring commitments to that produces a schedule that collapses by November, usually taking the useful two down with it. Choosing the two subjects where a grade is genuinely at risk, protecting those slots for a full term, and reviewing at the end is a better use of the same budget than spreading it thin.

faqs.question: Does a visiting tutor come to our villa, or is this all online?
faqs.answer: All of it is online. IB Gram does not send tutors into households anywhere in the United Arab Emirates; visiting a student's address is a service we run only in India, and that does not change for a particular community or a particular fee. Sessions are one-to-one over live video at a fixed slot in Gulf Standard Time, with a shared whiteboard, a document camera for handwritten working, and a recording that goes to the family. If your requirement is specifically an adult physically in the room, which is fair for a young child, we are the wrong provider and would rather say so now.

faqs.question: How do we know what was covered if we were not in the room?
faqs.answer: Three artefacts, all of them more durable than overhearing. A shared running document, updated during the session rather than afterwards, holding what was taught and what was set. A recording of the hour, which a parent can sample rather than watch in full. And marked work returned to you with dropped marks circled and the mark scheme's own wording beside each, plus a one-page note every fortnight saying what moved and what did not. Together those answer a question presence never quite does, which is whether anything is changing rather than whether the room sounded busy.

faqs.question: Is it worth using the summer between DP1 and DP2?
faqs.answer: It is the single best-value window in the programme and the least used. Six to eight weeks with no teaching, no homework and every internal deadline still ahead. The highest-return use is coursework: getting an exploration or a scientific investigation to a genuine first draft and settling an Extended Essay research question, all of which otherwise land in the autumn alongside mock examinations. The second-best use is closing one content gap from DP1. Two sessions a week for six weeks, then a deliberate stop, is the shape that works. Households who use this window describe DP2 as busy rather than impossible.

faqs.question: What happens to the recordings of my child's lessons?
faqs.answer: They go to the family and are held so the student can revise from them and a parent can review them. They are not published, not used as marketing material, and nothing identifiable about a child appears on this site. They can be deleted on request. The reason this paragraph exists is Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on the Protection of Personal Data, which almost no page in this market mentions while nearly all of them collect a child's name, school, year group and grades through a form. A privacy link belongs on every page that carries one, including this page.

faqs.question: Can two children in the same household share a timetable?
faqs.answer: They can share an evening without sharing a tutor, which is the arrangement that actually works. Two students at different Diploma years need two specialists, and the in-home model pushes families towards one tutor covering both because a second visit means a second journey. Online, the sessions simply sit back to back with two plans, two diagnostics and two notes. This is the most common booking shape in Khalifa City and Al Shamkha, where villa households often have two or three school-age children, and it keeps the convenience of one evening without the compromise of one generalist.

faqs.question: When is it right to pause rather than push through?
faqs.answer: School mock examination week is a clear pause: an extra session the night before produces fatigue rather than marks. A genuine family event is another. What matters is that the pause has a restart date agreed when it begins. A pause with a date in the diary costs nothing and sessions not taken are not charged. A pause described as a few weeks costs most of a term, because the slot gets released, the habit breaks and the restart conversation keeps being deferred. In the second term of DP2 the right answer is almost always to shorten rather than suspend.

faqs.question: Do the Arabic and Islamic Education lessons at school affect our plan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and most non-Arab parents underestimate them. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must follow the Ministry's general regulations, so those subjects occupy timetabled hours and set homework alongside the Diploma. Dubai's published guidance, the most detailed public statement of how this works, also requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in several of them. The household consequence is simple: count the real weekly commitment in September rather than discovering in January that the evenings were already full.

faqs.question: What does a term review tell us that a monthly update does not?
faqs.answer: Whether the hours bought anything. A term review sets the first diagnostic beside the most recent comparable one and compares the recurring-error count from the log, which is the only honest measure available. A monthly update tells you what was covered, which is activity rather than progress. Where the review shows little movement, the useful responses are specific: change the tutor because the match is wrong, change the rhythm because the problem was volume and was being treated as understanding, or stop. We will say which we think it is rather than renewing quietly.

faqs.question: How quickly can a household start, and what do you need from us?
faqs.answer: Two to five days for the common Diploma subjects, and the free trial lesson can usually be sat within the week. Send four things: the subject and level exactly as the school entered them, the most recent report or mock mark, one piece of work a teacher has already annotated, and the evening window that genuinely exists in your household rather than the one that sounds reasonable. The last of those is the item that decides whether the arrangement is still running in March, and it is the one families answer optimistically.

abu-dhabi/ib-home-tuition.closingHeading: Build the timetable first, then choose the tutor
abu-dhabi/ib-home-tuition.closingBody: Count the evenings that genuinely exist in your household, pick the two subjects where a grade is actually at risk, and fix a slot that will survive a full term rather than one that sounds like after school. Then send the subject and level as the school entered them, the latest mock mark and one annotated script, and the free trial lesson can be sat within the week. What follows is a term-by-term plan across both Diploma years, placed against your school's own internal deadlines, with Ramadan and summer travel agreed in advance. Sessions run one-to-one over live video into the household, on Gulf Standard Time, recorded, with a shared document you can read.

intro.heading: Why families type home tutor, and what they are usually asking for
paragraphs: Almost nobody searching for an IB home tutor in Abu Dhabi has strong feelings about the front door. What they want is four things bundled together: one adult giving their child undivided attention, a fixed time each week that does not depend on the child organising it, a parent able to tell whether anything is happening, and no additional driving in a city where the school run already eats an hour. Three of those four are properties of one-to-one teaching rather than of location.

The fourth, visibility, is the one families care about most and talk about least. Having a tutor in the dining room means a parent walking past can hear whether the hour is being used. That is a real benefit and it deserves a real replacement rather than a dismissal, which is why a later section of this page sets out exactly what substitutes for it: a recorded session, a shared running document, a marked script returned rather than described, and a written note every fortnight.

What in-home tutoring also brings is a cost structure nobody itemises. The Abu Dhabi market charges roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour for a visit, against AED 150 to 300 for a comparable qualified tutor online, and the gap is travel rather than teaching. A tutor who drives from Mussafah to Saadiyat for a 17:30 session has given up the better part of two hours and will price that in, openly or otherwise. You are paying for a car, in a city where the 17:00 band is the slowest hour of the day.

Then there is the pool problem, which is the one that actually decides outcomes. Abu Dhabi's Diploma cohort is smaller than Dubai's and spread across more schools, from the island cluster around Saadiyat and Al Bateen through the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor out to Al Shamkha and Zayed City. The number of people who can teach Chemistry HL to a high standard, hold a valid tutoring permit, live within a sensible drive of your community and are free at your preferred hour is frequently zero. The online pool is not.

So this page does both halves of the job. It answers the home-tutoring question with real figures, real drive times and the actual permit rules, because a family deciding between models deserves the information rather than a redirection. And it states the position without hedging: IB Gram does not send tutors into homes anywhere in the United Arab Emirates. That service exists only in India. Everything delivered to an Abu Dhabi family is one-to-one, over live video, on Gulf Standard Time, with the recording kept so the hour can be revisited. The rest of this page is written to be useful whichever model you choose at the end of it.

abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor.programmesIntro: The three IB programmes Abu Dhabi families ask about carry different reasons for wanting someone in the house. Primary parents want supervision. Middle Years parents want structure. Diploma parents want subject expertise they cannot find locally. Each needs a different answer, and only one of them is really about the front door.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and the service component. This is where the in-home model breaks down hardest, because what a DP student needs is someone who teaches that exact paper at that exact level, and geography is unrelated to whether such a person exists nearby. A sixteen-year-old also does not need supervision; they need a specialist.
programmes.countryNote: An Abu Dhabi DP student typically has a school day ending between 15:00 and 15:45, a commute, and mandatory UAE subject requirements running alongside the Diploma. A visiting tutor arriving at 17:30 after a cross-city drive gets a tired student at the worst hour. A video session can sit at 19:30 after food and a break, which is the single biggest scheduling advantage and the one nobody advertises.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Assessed on four criteria per subject, converted to a grade out of seven. The genuine need here is routine: a fixed hour, consistent expectations, and work that gets checked. Those are organisational properties, and a video session at a fixed slot delivers them as well as a visit does, provided the slot is actually fixed and not negotiated weekly.
programmes.countryNote: Middle Years parents in the emirate are the group most likely to want to overhear the lesson, and reasonably so at this age. The substitutes matter most here: a recorded session a parent can sample, a shared document showing what was set, and a short written note. Those give a clearer picture than overhearing half a conversation through a door.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: No external examinations, so the work is narrow by design: number fluency, reading, handwriting and written expression in short sessions. Attention span sets the length rather than the syllabus, and twenty-five to thirty-five minutes is usually the honest maximum for a seven-year-old regardless of where the adult is sitting.
programmes.countryNote: This is the one age band where the in-home case is strongest, because a young child needs an adult physically managing the session. Where a family's requirement is genuinely supervision of a primary-age child, a visiting tutor may be the right answer and we will say so. IB Gram does not provide that in the UAE, and pretending otherwise would waste your time.

programmes.name: Curriculum transitions into the IB
programmes.description: Students arriving into an Abu Dhabi IB school from CBSE, the American system, the British curriculum or a national system elsewhere carry specific, mappable gaps rather than general weakness. The work is a subject-by-subject audit against the IB course they have joined, then a short block closing the named differences. It is finite and it should be quoted as finite.
programmes.countryNote: Mid-year arrivals are common in Abu Dhabi because of posting cycles, and a student joining DP1 in January has missed a term of a two-year course. That is an urgent, bounded piece of work with a deadline attached, and it is the single most common reason a family wants someone in the house immediately. A specialist available this week over video beats a generalist available tomorrow in person.

abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Abu Dhabi families most often ask for by name when they search for in-home help, with the reason each one ends up on the list. In every case the limiting factor is whether a specialist in that paper exists and is free, not how far they would have to drive.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL
subjects.description: The most requested single course in the emirate and the one where generalist help does least. Proof, complex numbers and the harder calculus are not teachable by someone who last saw them at A-Level. Handwritten working is central, which is why a document camera matters more than physical proximity.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and regression with a graphing calculator assumed throughout. Screen sharing is genuinely better than sitting side by side here, because the tutor can see the calculator output and the spreadsheet at the same time rather than leaning over a shoulder.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms carry the mark spread, and the scientific investigation is worth 20 per cent of the grade across four criteria. The practical work happens in the school laboratory either way; the analysis and evaluation are where a tutor earns their hour.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Extended-response derivations are where marks go missing, usually because a correct physical idea is asserted without the algebra the mark scheme wants. Specialists at Higher Level are thin on the ground in the emirate, which is exactly why insisting on a local visit narrows the field to almost nothing.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content volume rather than conceptual difficulty, and marks lost to command terms: describing when the paper asked for an explanation or a comparison. Data-based questions are the most coachable part of the course and are usually the least practised at home.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Unseen analysis, a comparative essay, the individual oral and, at HL, the HL essay. The oral is rehearsable and therefore the component where preparation pays most reliably. Rehearsing it over video has an advantage: the recording lets the student hear themselves.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Management
subjects.description: Both lost on evaluation rather than knowledge. A diagram with correct axes and an explained shift earns marks prose will not, and the top band needs a judgement that chooses. Marking a paragraph line by line is identical work on a shared screen and on a kitchen table.

subjects.name: Arabic and the mandatory UAE subjects
subjects.description: Abu Dhabi students carry Arabic alongside the IB because the federal baseline requires Arabic, social studies and Islamic studies in private schools. Support has to distinguish between the school's mandatory stream and any separate examined qualification, because they are not the same syllabus.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Worth up to three bonus points between them. The Extended Essay is marked out of 34 with critical thinking alone carrying 12, and the Theory of Knowledge essay has a 1,600-word ceiling. Both are read-and-annotate work rather than taught content, which is well suited to written feedback.

abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor.regionsTitle: Abu Dhabi communities and what a visiting tutor would have faced
abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor.regionsIntro: These seven communities generate most of the in-home enquiries in the emirate. The notes describe the journey a visiting tutor would have made and what that does to the hour, because that cost is real whether or not anyone itemises it on an invoice. Sessions themselves run over live video from all of them.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Central to the school corridor and therefore the easiest community for a visiting tutor to reach, which is why in-home rates quoted here sit at the lower end. It is also the single largest source of Diploma enquiries, so the subject-specialist shortage bites hardest.

regions.name: Al Reef and Al Samha
regions.note: Out towards the Dubai road, far enough that a city-based tutor is committing well over an hour of driving for a one-hour session. Families here are quoted the top of the in-home range, and availability collapses to whoever already lives in the community.

regions.name: Zayed City and Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: Large, grid-planned and well inland. A tutor coming from the island faces the full 17:00 outbound queue in both directions, which in practice means the session either starts late or starts at 19:00. Video removes the choice entirely.

regions.name: Al Shamkha and Al Falah
regions.note: Fast-growing villa communities with young families and a thin local tutor pool. The honest in-home answer here is that the subject specialist a Diploma student needs almost certainly does not live within reach, and a generalist who does is not a substitute.

regions.name: Shakhbout City
regions.note: Between the mainland communities and the airport road, with a mixed school catchment. Sibling bookings are common, and consecutive video slots work better than a visit because two children on different programmes need different tutors, not one compromise.

regions.name: Mussafah and Baniyas
regions.note: Industrial and residential mix with long cross-city journeys to the island schools. Students here are often at schools some distance from home already, so adding a tutor's commute to the family's own is the least appealing part of the in-home model.

regions.name: Yas Island and Al Raha Beach
regions.note: Short hops to the Khalifa City schools but an awkward inbound journey from the city centre. Evening slots after 19:30 dominate here, and a recorded session matters because the hour sits late in a long day.

schoolClusters.city: The Khalifa City and Al Raha school corridor
schoolClusters.note: Where most of the emirate's IB and British provision sits, and where a visiting tutor's journey is shortest. Students we support from these schools usually ask for a named Diploma subject at a named level, which is a specialist request rather than a supervision request.

schoolClusters.city: The island schools: Saadiyat, Al Bateen and the Corniche
schoolClusters.note: A long drive from the mainland communities where many families actually live, which is the practical reason in-home quotes for these addresses sit high. Diploma departments here are experienced, and the usual request is a second opinion on a draft rather than content teaching.
schools: American Community School of Abu Dhabi

schoolClusters.city: Al Reem Island, Yas Island and the mainland communities
schoolClusters.note: Newer schools with growing cohorts and a high proportion of mid-year arrivals. The thin local tutor pool in these communities is the clearest argument against an in-home requirement, because the specialist a student needs lives somewhere else by definition.

modes.description: The default. A fixed slot in Gulf Standard Time, one tutor, one subject at one level, with a shared whiteboard and a document camera so handwritten working is visible in both directions. Sessions are recorded. No travel time appears in the rate because none is incurred, which is most of the price difference against a visit.

modes.title: Short intensive block over video
modes.description: Two or three sessions a week for four to six weeks, used before a mock, before an internal coursework deadline, or to close a gap left by a mid-year arrival. Finite by design and quoted as finite. The first session is a timed diagnostic rather than teaching, because a block this short cannot afford a wrong starting point.

modes.title: In-home visiting, for completeness
modes.description: The model this search describes, offered by independent tutors and agencies across the emirate at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour. It genuinely suits a primary-age child who needs an adult managing the session. IB Gram does not provide it anywhere in the UAE, and a family whose requirement is specifically a person in the room should know that before they spend another click here.

sections.heading: What an in-home IB tutor costs in Abu Dhabi, and what the travel adds
paragraphs: Most pages ranking for this search publish no figure at all, and two of them quote United States dollars. Here is the market in dirhams, with each range attributed. Bestimate's 2026 rate table for the UAE puts in-home tutoring at AED 180 to 350 an hour, with independent home tutors going to AED 500. A qualified subject tutor working online sits at AED 150 to 300, and Unitors lists IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. Specialists run AED 200 to 450 and upwards, with TutorChase publishing AED 270 and BartyED AED 650 for a premium named tutor.

The difference between those two bands is not teaching quality and it is not seniority. It is a car. A tutor driving from the island to Al Reef for a 17:30 hour has committed somewhere between ninety minutes and two hours of unpaid time to a sixty-minute lesson, and no rational person absorbs that. It is recovered in the rate, in a minimum booking length, or in a quiet preference for students who live nearby, which is how a family ends up with the closest tutor rather than the right one.

Monthly packages visible in the market make the gap concrete. Around AED 799 a month buys eight online sessions. In-home packages of four two-hour visits are advertised at AED 1,599 to 1,799. Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour session run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist examination-year support. None of these is an IB Gram price. We publish no rate card on these pages: the free trial lesson and the conversation after it are where a quote comes from.

sections.heading: The Abu Dhabi drive, and what it does to a 17:00 start
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi is laid out as an island city with a mainland that keeps extending, which produces long, predictable journeys rather than short unpredictable ones. A tutor who lives on the island and teaches in Al Shamkha is committing to a real expedition, and the hour between 17:00 and 18:00 is when everyone else is making the same trip in the opposite direction. The table below is a planning assumption, not a measurement, and it should be checked against your own experience of the route at the hour you want.

What the drive does to the lesson is the part worth thinking about. A tutor who arrives nine minutes late has lost nine minutes of a paid hour, and will usually still leave on time because another student is waiting. A tutor who hits an unusually bad run arrives at 17:50 for a 17:30 session with a student whose attention is already gone. Across a term, a weekly session losing ten minutes to traffic has lost most of a lesson, and nobody records it anywhere.

The second-order effect is on the slot itself. In-home scheduling pushes sessions towards the earliest hour the tutor can physically manage after their own working day, which is frequently the worst hour for the student: straight off a school bus, before food, in the heat. Video scheduling has no travel constraint, so a session can sit at 19:30 after a break and a meal. Of all the arguments for online delivery in this emirate, that one produces the most visible difference in the first fortnight.

sections.heading: Is your tutor legally permitted to teach in Abu Dhabi?
paragraphs: This is the question almost nobody asks and the one with the clearest answer. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 Regarding the Introduction of Private Tuition Work Permits, and is granted free of charge for two years through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. The ministry's own service page is titled Issuance of a New Work Permit for Private Tutor Licensing, lists no fee, states a two-working-day completion time, and is applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website or e-services system.

The eligibility list is broader than most families assume. It includes teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18. So a university student tutoring GCSE mathematics in the evening is not operating outside the system by definition, provided they hold the permit. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from the ministry are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws.

Two cautions belong here. No fine schedule is published, and a figure circulating online could not be verified against any official source, so no amount should be quoted to you by anyone, including us. And a tutoring operation with premises and staff is a different legal animal from an individual tutor: in Dubai that requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute. Nobody should describe themselves as approved by a regulator unless they hold the specific permit and can show the number. IB Gram holds no regulator approval, accreditation or licence of any kind, and says so.

sections.heading: The ethics rule that makes your child's own teacher the wrong choice
paragraphs: The most common in-home arrangement in this market is also the most problematic: paying a teacher at the child's own school. It is attractive for obvious reasons. They know the scheme of work, they know the cohort, and they may be the person who writes the predicted grade. That last point is the problem rather than the attraction.

ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff have been reported as prohibiting teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit carries a code of conduct that also bars serving students affiliated with the teacher's own school. This is press-reported rather than quoted from the policy document itself, so verify the current wording against ADEK before relying on it. The structural point does not depend on the citation: the person assessing your child should not also be invoicing you.

There is a quieter benefit to an outside tutor that families discover afterwards. A student who has misunderstood something taught by their own teacher often will not say so to that teacher, because the admission carries a social cost in a classroom they return to on Monday. A different adult, marking against the published criteria rather than against their own lesson, gets a straighter answer about what is not understood. That independence is worth more than familiarity with the scheme of work, which any competent subject specialist can reconstruct from the student's own exercise book.

sections.heading: Online against in-home for an Abu Dhabi household
paragraphs: Here is the comparison without the sales layer. In-home visiting wins on three things: physical management of a young child, a parent's ability to overhear, and the absence of any technology to go wrong. Online wins on pool size, scheduling freedom, cost, the existence of a recording, and the fact that nobody is in a car at 17:30 in August. For a Diploma student the second list decides it; for a seven-year-old the first list might.

The pool argument deserves a number rather than an adjective. Abu Dhabi's Diploma cohort is spread across many schools, and the subset of qualified specialists for any given Higher Level subject who also live within a reasonable drive of a specific community and are free at a specific hour is frequently empty. A family that insists on physical attendance has not chosen a better tutor; they have chosen from a shorter list, and in Higher Level Physics or a Group 2 language that list may contain nobody at all.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, or anywhere else in the UAE. Visiting households is a service we run only in India. That is stated on every country page on this site and it is not softened here. If your requirement is specifically that an adult sits in the room, the honest answer is that we are not the right provider, and the market rates in the first table of this page will help you negotiate with one who is.

sections.heading: Supervision without a stranger in the sitting room
paragraphs: The real loss when a tutor is not physically present is parental visibility, and it deserves a concrete replacement rather than reassurance. Four things do the job, and all four are better evidence than overhearing a lesson through a door. Sessions are recorded, so a parent can sample ten minutes of any hour they paid for rather than inferring from tone. A shared running document holds what was taught and what was set, so nothing depends on a teenager's account of it.

Marked work is returned rather than described. A script with dropped marks circled and the mark scheme's own phrasing written beside each is something a parent can hold, compare against the same exercise six weeks earlier, and show to a subject teacher. And a one-page note every fortnight says what moved, what did not and what the next fortnight targets, written for a parent who does not teach the subject.

Those four together answer a question that sitting in the room never quite does: is this working? A parent listening at the door learns whether the tutor is talkative and whether the child sounds engaged. Neither correlates reliably with marks. A dated pair of timed scripts four weeks apart, plus an error log showing the same mistakes disappearing, answers the question directly. The visibility is different in kind, and in practice it is more useful, because it is dated, comparable and written down rather than recalled afterwards from a doorway.

sections.heading: What a parent sitting in on a lesson actually learns
paragraphs: It is worth being precise about this, because it is the emotional centre of the in-home preference. A parent present for a lesson learns three things reliably: whether the tutor turned up, whether the hour was used, and whether their child seems comfortable. Those matter. A tutor who spends twenty minutes on small talk is easy to detect from the next room, and families who have been through a bad arrangement are right to want that tripwire.

What presence does not reveal is whether the teaching is correct. A confident explanation of a Chemistry mechanism sounds exactly like a confident wrong explanation of one, and no parent who does not teach the subject can tell them apart from the hallway. Nor does presence show whether the hour was pointed at the right thing. A tutor working patiently through a topic the student already understands sounds productive and is wasting the term.

That is why the substitutes above are designed around marked work rather than around observation. A recording covers the attendance-and-effort question that presence answers. The marked script and the error log answer the correctness-and-direction questions that presence never could. Families who move from an in-home arrangement to this one usually report the same thing after a month: they see less and know more. That is an unfamiliar trade, and for a student old enough to manage their own session it is the right one, because the thing a parent needs to know is whether marks are moving rather than whether the room sounded busy.

sections.heading: Honest limits on assessed work and materials
paragraphs: The in-home market in this region contains some of the worst practice in the sector, and a page about home tutoring has an obligation to name it. At least one site ranking for these searches sells completed Internal Assessments. Buying one is malpractice under IB rules and the consequence falls on the student's own certification, not on the vendor. Proximity makes this worse rather than better: a tutor in the house, unsupervised, with a deadline on Monday, is the exact situation in which the line gets crossed quietly.

The permissible version is narrow and worth stating. A tutor teaches the skill the task assesses. A tutor explains what each criterion rewards and how many marks it carries. A tutor reads a draft the student has produced and writes down what the criteria would credit and refuse. The student then revises it, in their own words, with their own judgements. Nothing assessed is authored, supplied or edited to completion, and feedback is written rather than spoken so a supervisor or a parent can see exactly what was said.

Materials follow the same rule. Syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to the IB, Cambridge and Pearson. They are referenced, linked and used on screen from the official source rather than reproduced as downloads or redistributed as files. That is the lawful position and it also means the student is working from the real document rather than from somebody's retyped version of it, which is a more common problem than families expect.

No assessed work is authored, supplied or edited to completion

sections.heading: Booking, and the coverage position stated up front
paragraphs: Send three things: the subject and level exactly as the school entered them, the most recent report or mock mark, and one piece of work a teacher has already annotated. The third is the one families leave out and the one that shortens the diagnosis most, because a teacher's own marks on a real script show how the department reads the work rather than how a single grade summarises a whole term of it.

The free trial lesson is a real lesson with the tutor who would teach the course, booked without card details. What it tests is whether your child will admit to this particular adult that they do not understand something. No amount of credential-reading answers that, and it is the single best predictor of whether the arrangement will produce anything.

Coverage is stated before you pay. Mathematics at either level, the three sciences, English A, Economics and Business Management are reasonably covered in UAE evening hours, with 17:00 to 19:00 the tightest band because every family wants it. Group 2 languages beyond French and Spanish take longer. Higher Level Further Mathematics, Design Technology and Music are genuinely thin, and where nothing suitable is free you are told so and offered a later slot, a wait, or a straight no. No competitor page in this market discloses a coverage limit at all, and several route UAE parents to a non-UAE phone number without ever mentioning where the tutor actually sits.

process.title: Tell us the subject, the level and your real evening window
process.description: Not the window you would like, the one that exists after the school run, food and a younger sibling's bedtime. In most Abu Dhabi households that is later than families first suggest, and a slot set honestly at 19:30 survives a term where an optimistic 17:15 collapses inside a fortnight.

process.title: Free trial lesson with the tutor who would teach
process.description: A real lesson on real content, with the person who would take the course rather than a coordinator, booked without card details. It answers the one question credentials cannot: whether your child will say out loud, to this particular adult, that they are lost.

process.title: A timed diagnostic before any teaching
process.description: Session one is a past-paper section at the correct level, marked against the published mark scheme while your child watches. It produces an error log classified by topic and command term, which becomes the planning document. Teaching that starts before this exists is teaching aimed at a described problem rather than a real one.

process.title: Visibility set up deliberately, not improvised
process.description: Recording on, shared document created, marked work returned to you rather than described, and a fortnightly note scheduled. These are the four substitutes for sitting in the room, and they work only if they are set up in week one rather than promised and forgotten.

process.title: A term review you can act on
process.description: At the end of a term the first diagnostic sits beside the latest one and the recurring-error count is compared. Where the comparison shows little movement, the useful options are a different tutor, a different approach, or stopping. We will say which we think it is rather than letting the arrangement drift.

whyPoints.title: The home-tutoring question answered, not deflected
whyPoints.description: Real market rates with sources, real drive times, the actual permit rules and the ethics position on a child's own teacher. A family comparing models deserves the information even where it points somewhere other than us, and the first table on this page is useful whoever you end up hiring.

whyPoints.title: No travel in the rate, because none is incurred
whyPoints.description: The gap between AED 180-500 for a visit and AED 150-300 for a qualified online tutor is mostly a car. Removing the journey removes the premium, the late arrival, the traffic cancellation and the quiet preference for students who happen to live close to the tutor.

whyPoints.title: A pool chosen by subject, not by postcode
whyPoints.description: For Higher Level Physics or a Group 2 language, the set of specialists within a drive of Al Shamkha who are free at 18:00 can be empty. Choosing by the paper the student sits rather than by distance is the single biggest determinant of whether the hours are worth anything.

whyPoints.title: Visibility by artefact
whyPoints.description: A recording to sample, a shared document, a marked script returned to you, an error log and a fortnightly one-page note. Parents who move from an in-home arrangement usually say the same thing after a month: they see less and know more.

whyPoints.title: The assessed-work line stated plainly
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches, questions and annotates; the student writes. Nothing assessed is authored, supplied or edited to completion, and the feedback is written down so a supervisor can audit it. In a market where finished Internal Assessments are openly on sale, this is a real difference rather than a slogan.

whyPoints.title: Coverage disclosed before payment
whyPoints.description: Where no specialist is free in UAE evening hours, you are told before booking and offered a later slot, a wait, or nothing. Filling a Further Mathematics HL request with a generalist produces a cancelled arrangement in week three and a wasted month in between.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a tutor to our house in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No. Visiting households is a service IB Gram runs only in India, and it is not offered anywhere in the United Arab Emirates. Everything delivered to an Abu Dhabi family is one-to-one and runs over live video on Gulf Standard Time. That position is stated on every country page on this site rather than buried here. If your requirement is specifically that an adult is physically present, which is a fair requirement for a young child, we are not the right provider and the market rates published on this page will help you negotiate with someone who is.

faqs.question: How much does an in-home IB tutor charge in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour. Bestimate's 2026 UAE rate table puts in-home tutoring at AED 180 to 350, with independent home tutors reaching AED 500. Monthly in-home packages of four two-hour visits are advertised at AED 1,599 to 1,799. By comparison a qualified subject tutor online sits at AED 150 to 300, with Unitors listing IB from AED 200 and TutorChase AED 270. The difference between the two bands is travel rather than teaching quality. Those are market figures from published sources with the date attached, not an IB Gram price list.

faqs.question: Why is a visiting tutor more expensive if the lesson is the same length?
faqs.answer: Because the lesson is not what you are paying for in full. A tutor driving from Al Bateen to Al Reef for a 17:30 hour has committed ninety minutes to two hours of unpaid travel to a sixty-minute booking, and that time is recovered somewhere: in the hourly rate, in a minimum booking length, or in an unspoken preference for students who live nearby. The last version is the expensive one, because it quietly narrows your choice of tutor to whoever is geographically convenient rather than whoever teaches the paper your child sits.

faqs.question: Does my child's tutor need a UAE permit, and can I ask to see it?
faqs.answer: Yes to both. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, whose service page is titled Issuance of a New Work Permit for Private Tutor Licensing and lists a two-working-day completion time. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring without it is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so be wary of any quoted amount.

faqs.question: Can we hire the teacher who actually teaches my son at his school?
faqs.answer: It is the most common arrangement in this market and the most problematic. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff have been reported as prohibiting paid private tutoring of students enrolled at the teacher's own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct is reported to bar the same thing. Verify the current wording with ADEK before relying on it. The structural objection stands anyway: the person who writes your son's predicted grade should not also be invoicing you, and a student rarely admits confusion to the teacher they face again on Monday.

faqs.question: My daughter is in Al Shamkha. Would a local tutor even cover Physics HL?
faqs.answer: Probably not, and this is the clearest practical argument on the page. Abu Dhabi's Diploma cohort is spread across many schools, and the set of people who can teach Higher Level Physics to a high standard, hold a valid permit, live within a sensible drive of Al Shamkha and are free at 18:00 is frequently empty. A family insisting on physical attendance in that situation has not chosen a better tutor; they have chosen from a much shorter list, and sometimes from a list of one generalist. Online, the pool is everyone who teaches that paper.

faqs.question: How do I know the hour is being used if nobody is in the room?
faqs.answer: Four substitutes, all of them stronger evidence than overhearing a lesson. Sessions are recorded, so you can sample ten minutes of any hour you paid for. A shared document holds what was taught and what was set, so nothing depends on a teenager's summary. Marked scripts are returned to you rather than described, with dropped marks circled and the mark scheme's own wording beside each. And a one-page note every fortnight says what moved and what did not. Presence tells you whether a tutor is talkative. A dated pair of marked scripts tells you whether anything changed.

faqs.question: Is a visiting tutor better for a primary-age child?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, and it would be dishonest to argue otherwise. A six- or seven-year-old needs an adult physically managing the session: keeping them at the table, controlling the materials, handling the fifteen-minute attention ceiling. A video call demands self-regulation a young child does not reliably have, and a parent ends up supervising the supervision. Where that is the requirement, an in-home tutor at the market rates published on this page is a sensible purchase. IB Gram does not provide it in the UAE, and saying so now saves you a conversation later.

faqs.question: What equipment does my son need at home for a video session?
faqs.answer: Less than families expect. A laptop with a working microphone, a reliable connection, and some way to show handwritten working: a phone on a cheap stand pointed at the page, or a tablet with a stylus. For Mathematics and the sciences the handwriting channel matters more than video quality, because a tutor needs to see the working as it is produced rather than the finished answer. Headphones help in an apartment. A second screen is useful at Higher Level but not necessary. Nothing on that list costs more than a single in-home session at the market rate.

faqs.question: What happens to the session if the internet drops mid-lesson?
faqs.answer: The tutor reconnects, usually within a minute, and the lost time is made up at the end or in the following session. This is a smaller failure mode than it sounds, and worth comparing with its in-home equivalent: a tutor stuck in the 17:00 traffic does not arrive late and continue, they lose the first fifteen minutes and leave on time because another student is waiting. Where a connection genuinely fails, the session is rescheduled rather than charged. Recordings mean a partially completed session still leaves something usable behind.

faqs.question: Can sessions move to post-Iftar timing during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and arranging it in advance works better than improvising week by week. Most Abu Dhabi families shift to a later and shorter slot after Iftar, and because there is no travel involved the move costs nothing and does not depend on a tutor's willingness to drive at an awkward hour. The plan is compressed rather than paused, which matters because school-set internal deadlines for Internal Assessments and the Extended Essay do not move for the calendar. Agree the pattern before the month starts and the term survives it.

faqs.question: Will a tutor sit with my child while they finish their Internal Assessment?
faqs.answer: A tutor will teach the skill the task assesses, explain what each criterion rewards and how many marks it carries, read a draft your child has produced, and write down what the criteria would credit and refuse in it. Your child then revises it themselves, in their own words. What never happens is authoring, supplying or editing assessed work to completion. The proximity question is relevant here: an unsupervised adult in the house with a deadline on Monday is exactly the situation in which that line gets crossed quietly, which is one reason written feedback is the safer format.

faqs.question: We have two children on different IB programmes. Does that work online?
faqs.answer: Better than it works in person, which is the counterintuitive part. Two children at different stages need two different specialists, and an in-home arrangement pushes a family towards one tutor who will cover both because a second visit means a second journey. Online, the sessions simply sit back to back in the evening with two different tutors, two separate plans, two diagnostics and two notes. Sibling bookings are common in Khalifa City and Shakhbout City for exactly this reason, and the convenience of one timetable no longer requires the compromise of one generalist.

faqs.question: How quickly can we start, and what if nobody covers our subject?
faqs.answer: Two to five days for the common subjects: Mathematics at either level, the three sciences, English A, Economics and Business Management. The 17:00 to 19:00 band is the tightest because every family wants it, so a later slot often starts sooner. Group 2 languages beyond French and Spanish take one to three weeks. Higher Level Further Mathematics, Design Technology and Music are genuinely thin and can be unavailable, in which case you are told that before booking and offered a later slot, a wait, or nothing at all rather than a generalist.

faqs.question: What do you actually need from us before the first paid session?
faqs.answer: Three documents and one honest answer. The subject and level exactly as the school entered them, because Higher and Standard Level are different courses and the school's entry is the only reliable record. The most recent report or mock mark. One piece of work a teacher has already annotated, which tells a tutor more in five minutes than a term of grades. And the evening window that genuinely exists in your household after the school run, food and a younger child's bedtime, rather than the one that sounds reasonable in an email.

abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor.closingHeading: Compare the models properly, then book a trial
abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor.closingBody: If you came here for an in-home tutor, the figures on this page are yours to use with whoever you hire: AED 180 to 500 an hour from the published market tables, travel inside the rate, and a permit you are entitled to ask to see. If the real requirement was a specialist in your child's actual subject at a time that fits an Abu Dhabi evening, send the subject, the level and your honest window. The free trial lesson is a real lesson with the tutor who would teach, booked without card details, and the coverage position for your subject is stated before anything is paid. Sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time.

abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor-fees.tutorsIntro: Profiles below show the courses and levels each tutor teaches. Fees in this market track level and scarcity far more closely than they track experience in years, so read the level first: Higher Level cover is priced differently from Standard Level in every provider's rate card.

intro.heading: A quote is four costs wearing one number
paragraphs: When a tutor in Abu Dhabi says AED 350 an hour, that figure is carrying several things at once and the proportions change dramatically depending on where you live. Part of it is the teaching hour itself. Part of it is the time the tutor spends driving to Saadiyat or out to Al Reef and back, which is unpaid unless it is inside the rate. Part of it is the marking and preparation done between sessions, which some tutors include and others quietly do not. And part of it is the risk the tutor carries on cancellations, which is why a flexible arrangement always costs more per hour than a committed term.

Market figures for this emirate are reasonably well established even though almost nobody publishes them. In-home one-to-one tuition in the UAE runs roughly AED 180 to AED 350 an hour in Bestimate's 2026 survey of tutoring costs, with independent home tutors quoting AED 200 to AED 500. Qualified tutors working online sit at roughly AED 150 to AED 300, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. Budget platforms start lower: EdFlik from AED 45 to AED 65, Tutopiya from AED 33 to AED 52. Specialist IB and A Level cover runs AED 200 to AED 450 and above, TutorChase publishes AED 270 and BartyED AED 650. None of these are IB Gram prices; they are the market you are shopping in.

The gap between the in-home band and the online band is not a quality gap. It is mostly a transport gap. A tutor crossing from the mainland to the island for a single 60-minute lesson has committed two to two and a half hours of their working day, and no rational person prices that at one hour. Understanding this makes the whole market legible: the premium you pay for a visit buys presence in the room, not better teaching, and the same money buys more teaching hours or a scarcer specialist if you remove the car from the equation.

There is a second thing fees are quietly buying, and it is the one parents most often fail to ask about. A session where the tutor has already read and marked the student's work is a different product from a session where the first twenty minutes are spent finding out what happened last week. The first costs the tutor unbilled time and shows up as a higher hourly figure. The second looks cheaper per hour and delivers perhaps two thirds of the teaching. Ask explicitly whether marking between sessions is included, because the answer separates two things being sold at similar prices.

The rest of this page prices the pieces. A rate card by programme and level with the in-home and online columns side by side. A travel table for the real Abu Dhabi corridors, because a Khalifa City family and an Al Khalidiyah family are not shopping in the same market. What a 60 and a 90-minute session can actually finish, by assessment component. Tuition set against school fees and examination entry. And the extras that appear on a second invoice. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, which is also why there is no travel line in anything we quote.
