sections.heading: ADEK, inspection ratings, and how to read your school's report
paragraphs: In Abu Dhabi and Al Ain, private schools are licensed and inspected by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which the UAE government describes as supervising the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. That is a different authority from Dubai's KHDA and from Sharjah's SPEA, and the distinction matters for Al Wahda parents because advice written for Dubai often does not apply here.

An inspection report is the single most useful free document a parent has, and most never open it past the headline band. The body of the report tells you something a band cannot: which subjects and which year groups the inspectors judged weaker, how the school performed on progress rather than attainment, and what it was told to improve since the last visit. A school rated well overall can still carry a specific weakness in Diploma sciences, and that weakness is exactly what a tutor is for.

Read your report with three questions. Where did inspectors say progress lagged attainment, because that is where able children are coasting? What did the report say about the Diploma or the secondary phase specifically, rather than the whole school? And which recommendations from the previous inspection were still outstanding? Three minutes of that beats an hour of discussing an overall grade.

One warning. No tutoring company is approved, licensed or endorsed by ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and we are not either. Naming a regulator and explaining what it does is useful. A tutoring site claiming a regulator's blessing is telling you something that is not true, and it is the most common false claim in this market.

sections.heading: Academic honesty while the clock is running on an IA
paragraphs: Deadline pressure is where academic honesty actually gets tested. A student three days from an Internal Assessment deadline with 1,200 words of a 2,000-word exploration is in the exact position where a dishonest offer looks like a lifeline, and this market contains providers who sell completed Internal Assessments outright. One of them advertises them at a fixed price. Buying that is malpractice under IB rules, and the consequence lands on the student, not the seller.

The legitimate line is clear enough to write down. A tutor may teach the underlying content, explain what each assessment criterion rewards, read a draft the student wrote and say which criterion is capping the mark, question a research question until it becomes answerable, and check that referencing meets the school's expectations. A tutor may not write any part of the piece, redraft sentences into their own prose, supply the data, or produce the work in any form.

In practice that distinction shows up in how a session ends. An honest IA hour ends with the student holding a list of things to go away and do. A dishonest one ends with a better document and a student who cannot explain how it got better. If your child cannot talk you through what changed and why, something has gone wrong regardless of what anyone promised.

This matters commercially as well as ethically. Schools in Abu Dhabi know the local market, coordinators read drafts they have seen develop, and the IB requires authenticity declarations. A paid-for IA is a risk to a student's entire Diploma. We would rather lose the booking than take it, and we say so plainly on every page.

sections.heading: Permits, Ramadan and the practical questions nobody answers
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, it is granted free of charge for two years, and the eligible categories include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time, and the application goes through the MoHRE app, website or e-services system.

Two things follow for a parent. First, anyone offering paid private lessons in the UAE should hold that permit, and operating without one carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so treat any specific figure you read as unverified. Second, in Abu Dhabi, professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from paid tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct points the same way. A tutor offering to privately coach your child in a subject they also teach them in class is offering something they should not.

Ramadan reshapes the academic term every year, and the shift is predictable even though the dates move. School days shorten, energy drops in the afternoon, and the useful tutoring slot moves to after Iftar. Families in Al Wahda who plan that shift in advance keep momentum through a month that otherwise eats four weeks of a Diploma run-in. Families who do not plan it usually lose the sessions altogether.

The last practical question is what happens when nobody is available. Some Higher Level subjects have genuinely thin coverage, and in that case we say so rather than putting a generalist in front of your child. Sometimes the honest answer is a specialist in another timezone whose evening is your afternoon, and sometimes it is that we cannot help this term. Both answers are better than a mismatch you discover in February.

process.title: Tell us the subject, the level and the next date
process.description: Not "maths help" but "Maths AA HL, mock in January, Paper 3 is the problem". The next fixed date in your child's school calendar does more to shape a plan than anything else you can tell us, and it takes a sentence to supply.

process.title: A free trial lesson with the proposed tutor
process.description: One real hour, teaching real content, with the teacher we think fits. You watch or you do not, as you prefer. At the end you get a short written read on where the gap actually is, and you decide whether to continue. No card details are needed to book it.

process.title: An eight-week plan in writing
process.description: What will be covered, in what order, and what your child will have produced by the end of it. Written in language a parent can check, including which school deadlines it is built around and where the plan pauses for school examination weeks.

process.title: Weekly sessions with marked work between them
process.description: The same tutor, the same slot, with work set at the end of each hour and marked before the next one starts. Scripts and notes are saved, so what happened in week three is still readable in week eight when the mock results arrive.

process.title: A review at the end, and an honest stop
process.description: We check the plan against what actually happened, and if the job is done we say so. Ongoing tuition that no longer has a target is how families end up paying for a habit. If a different subject now needs the hour more, we move it.

whyPoints.title: Matched to the level, not the neighbourhood
whyPoints.description: Maths AA HL, Maths AI SL and MYP extended maths are three different teaching jobs. We match on the exact course and level your child is sitting, which is why a central Abu Dhabi family is not limited to the people prepared to drive to Al Wahda this week.

whyPoints.title: The calendar drives the plan
whyPoints.description: Plans here are built backwards from the next fixed date in your child's school calendar: the mock window, the IA submission, the registration deadline. A plan that ignores those dates will be overtaken by them, however good the teaching inside it is.

whyPoints.title: Rates you can check against the market
whyPoints.description: Every AED figure on this page is a rate somebody else published, with the publisher named and the month it was read. Our own quote comes after a trial lesson, for your child's actual subject and frequency, so you can hold it against those bands.

whyPoints.title: A hard line on assessed work
whyPoints.description: Feedback on your child's own drafts, criterion by criterion, and nothing beyond that. We do not write, redraft or supply coursework, and we will explain why to any student who asks. In a market that contains sellers of completed Internal Assessments, that line is the product.

whyPoints.title: Delivery stated before you enquire
whyPoints.description: UAE lessons are one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. In-home visits are an India-only part of our service, and nobody is sent to an Abu Dhabi address. You know the format before you spend a minute on a form.

faqs.question: Can IB Gram send an IB home tutor to an apartment in Al Wahda?
faqs.answer: No. Home visits are a service we run only in India, and nobody is sent to an address in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE. Tuition for Al Wahda families is one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, on your child's own laptop. We state that before you enquire because a family who wants a person physically in the room deserves to know immediately. What the online format buys you is choice of teacher: the Higher Level specialist your child needs rather than whoever will drive into central Abu Dhabi at five o'clock.

faqs.question: Which IB examination session do Abu Dhabi Diploma students actually sit?
faqs.answer: Abu Dhabi schools run their Diploma cohorts to the May session. We deliberately do not publish exact IB examination or results dates on this page, because the IB issues the timetable to schools and your child's coordinator holds the authoritative version against the candidate number. Treat any tutoring site that quotes you a precise IB date as a source to check rather than trust. For Cambridge and Pearson qualifications the position is public: Cambridge runs June and November series for UAE centres, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November.

faqs.question: My child has just started DP1 at a central Abu Dhabi school. Is it too early for a tutor?
faqs.answer: It is the right time for the right kind of tutoring and the wrong time for exam technique. DP1 hours are well spent on the Higher Level foundations Year 13 will assume, on getting at least one Internal Assessment research question to something answerable, and on building the reading habit the Extended Essay needs. Those three things decide more of a final grade than any amount of past-paper drilling in the first year. Selling a DP1 student a paper-technique package in November is the most common way money gets wasted in this market.

faqs.question: What can eight weeks of tutoring realistically achieve for a DP2 student?
faqs.answer: One timed past paper per subject, properly marked and dissected rather than just completed. One Internal Assessment moved from an unmarked draft to a draft that has been read against the criteria. And one honest conversation about whether the current spread of Higher Levels is still right. That is a genuine eight weeks for a student who also has school, Creativity Activity Service and sleep. Anybody promising substantially more is either padding hours or ignoring the rest of your child's week.

faqs.question: How much should an Al Wahda family budget per month for IB tutoring?
faqs.answer: On published market rates, one weekly hour with a qualified subject tutor works out at roughly AED 600 to AED 1,200 a month, and an exam-year specialist nearer AED 1,000 to AED 2,000. Bestimate's 2026 rate work puts budget weekly tutoring at AED 240-600 monthly. Monthly packages advertised in this market include AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599-1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions. Those are other providers' numbers, read in October 2026. Our own quote follows a free trial lesson and reflects the actual subject, level and frequency.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with my daughter's Maths Analysis and Approaches Internal Assessment?
faqs.answer: Yes, within clear limits. A tutor can teach the mathematics involved, explain what each criterion rewards, interrogate the research question before any work is wasted, read a draft your daughter has written and say which criterion is holding the mark down, and check the referencing against her school's expectations. A tutor cannot write any part of the exploration, redraft her sentences, or supply the work. The test is simple: after the session she should be able to explain to you what she is going to change and why.

faqs.question: What does ADEK's inspection rating actually tell me about my child's school?
faqs.answer: Less than the report behind it. ADEK licenses and inspects private schools in Abu Dhabi and Al Ain, and the full report tells you which phases and subjects inspectors judged weaker, whether progress kept up with attainment, and what the school was told to improve last time. A school with a strong overall band can still carry a specific weakness in Diploma sciences. Read for the place where progress lagged attainment: that is usually where an able child is coasting, and it is exactly what tutoring is for.

faqs.question: Do private tutors in Abu Dhabi need a government permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day turnaround. Anyone tutoring for payment without the permit is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no fine schedule is published, so any specific amount you see quoted online is unverified.

faqs.question: Can Al Wahda sessions move to after Iftar during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and families who arrange it in advance keep their momentum through the month. School days shorten during Ramadan and afternoon concentration drops, so the useful slot moves to the evening after Iftar. Because lessons are online, moving the slot is a scheduling change rather than a logistics problem for anybody's driver. Al Wahda families in a Diploma year should fix the Ramadan timetable before the month begins; the alternative is usually four weeks of cancelled sessions at precisely the point when the run-in matters.

faqs.question: What happens if no tutor is available for Physics HL this term?
faqs.answer: We tell you, rather than putting a generalist in front of your child. Some Higher Level subjects genuinely have thin coverage in any given term, and the honest options are a specialist in another timezone whose evening falls in your child's afternoon, a short wait for a slot to open, or a straight no from us. All three beat a mismatch that you discover in February when the mock results come back. We would rather decline the booking than take it on and hope.

faqs.question: How late in DP2 can my child drop a subject from Higher to Standard Level?
faqs.answer: That is a school decision, not a tutoring one, and it is governed by the registration your coordinator submits inside IB deadlines. Practically, the window closes in Term 1 of DP2, which is why a level review belongs in the first eight weeks of that year rather than after the mocks. Ask your coordinator for the exact cut-off for your cohort. If the honest answer is that three Higher Levels was always one too many, no amount of tutoring substitutes for making that change in time.

faqs.question: Will a tutor follow my child's school scheme of work or a generic syllabus order?
faqs.answer: Your child's. The point of weekly one-to-one is that it moves at the pace of the actual class, so a gap gets caught in the week it appears instead of in the mock. That means we want the school's unit order, the dates of internal assessments and school examination weeks, and the teacher's own feedback where you have it. Tutoring that runs on a different timetable from the classroom produces a student doing two courses at once, which is more work and less progress.

faqs.question: My son has never had an online lesson. Will it work for him?
faqs.answer: The honest answer is that it works for most students and not for all, which is why the trial lesson exists. What makes it work is a quiet room, a laptop rather than a phone, headphones, and a tutor who shares a screen and writes on the work instead of talking at a camera. What breaks it is a tired student at nine o'clock, a shared living room, and a session with no task set at the end. Try one real hour and judge from that rather than from the idea of it.

faqs.question: What will my child need for UAE Ministry of Education equivalency after the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Equivalency is a Ministry process, not something a tutoring company performs or guarantees, and the requirements differ by curriculum. For the British route the published rule is five accredited IGCSE or GCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one A Level at E or two AS Levels. For the IB route we deliberately publish no points figure, because we have not read one on an official Ministry source. Verify your child's position with the Ministry's own channel.

abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor-in-al-wahda.closingHeading: Start with the next date in your child's calendar
abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor-in-al-wahda.closingBody: If your child is in DP2, the useful first message names the subject, the level and the next fixed date: a mock window, an Internal Assessment deadline, a registration cut-off. If your child is in DP1, say that instead, and we will plan foundations rather than sell technique. Either way the first hour is a free trial lesson with the teacher we think fits, taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and it ends with a short written read on where the gap actually sits. No payment details are needed to book it, and an Al Wahda family can have that hour inside the week.

intro.heading: Why the search for a home tutor in Al Zahiyah is really a search for a free hour
paragraphs: Al Zahiyah, the district Abu Dhabi residents still call the Tourist Club Area, is one of the densest residential pockets on the island. It runs between the Corniche and the channel that separates the island from Al Maryah, and it is built almost entirely of mid-rise and high-rise apartment blocks rather than villa compounds. That matters for tuition in a way no competitor page explains: there is no large international private school campus inside Al Zahiyah itself. Children who live here are enrolled at campuses in Al Bateen, Al Mushrif, Al Nahyan, Al Reem Island, or out on the mainland in Khalifa City and Al Raha, and they get there by bus.

Work backwards from that and the picture changes. A mainland campus is a twenty-five to forty-minute run from Al Zahiyah in morning traffic, which means a bus pick-up somewhere between 06:20 and 06:45 for a day that starts at 07:45. The teaching day on most Abu Dhabi secondary timetables finishes between 14:45 and 15:30. Add the return run and the bus door opens back in Al Zahiyah between 15:40 and 16:40. A Diploma student has eaten nothing substantial since a 06:00 breakfast and has three subjects' homework waiting.

Into that window, a parent is asked to fit a tutor who also has to drive somewhere. An in-home tutor covering the island charges for the journey, directly or indirectly, and arrives in the slot that works for their route rather than the slot that works for your child. If the tutor is coming from the mainland, the practical earliest arrival on the island on a weekday is around 17:30. If they are coming from elsewhere on the island, you are choosing from whoever happens to live within a short drive, which is a very small pool once the subject is narrowed to Higher Level Chemistry or Mathematics Analysis and Approaches.

Online one-to-one removes the journey from both sides of the arrangement. A session can start at 16:15 while a parent is still finishing work at Al Maryah or Al Mina, it can start at 19:30 after dinner, and during Ramadan it can move to a post-Iftar slot without renegotiating anybody's commute. More usefully, the tutor pool stops being geographic. A student at a Khalifa City campus studying Higher Level Economics is matched to someone who teaches Higher Level Economics, wherever that teacher sits, and who has read the same subject guide their school is working from.

This page answers the home-tutoring question honestly rather than deflecting it. It sets out what the Abu Dhabi in-home market charges and what the travel component of that figure actually pays for. It gives the commute arithmetic school by school so you can see which session times are real. It explains what ADEK does, what the MoHRE tutoring permit is, where Diploma marks tend to go missing, and exactly where a tutor's help on an Internal Assessment stops being help and starts being malpractice. Then it tells you what to do next, including what happens when nobody is free for the subject you need.

abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor-in-al-zahiyah.programmesIntro: The IB is four programmes, and an Al Zahiyah family may be inside any of them depending on which campus the bus goes to. The support a Primary Years child needs is not a smaller version of Diploma support, and the Middle Years assessment language is different again. Here is what each programme asks of a student, and what it tends to ask of a household on the island.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The Primary Years Programme is organised around transdisciplinary units of inquiry rather than discrete subject syllabuses. There is no external examination. Assessment is formative and continuous, built from learning portfolios, teacher observation and the Year 6 exhibition. Tutoring at this stage is about literacy and number fluency, English as an additional language where that applies, and helping a child articulate reasoning out loud, because the programme marks thinking as much as answers.
programmes.countryNote: Al Zahiyah's apartment blocks house a lot of early-primary children whose parents work on Al Maryah Island or at Al Mina, so the 15:40 bus often lands before either parent is home. Short online sessions of thirty to forty minutes at 16:30 suit this age group far better than an hour, and they fit the gap before a parent walks through the door.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The Middle Years Programme assesses eight subject groups against four criteria each, lettered A to D, and reports on a one-to-eight scale per criterion rather than a single percentage. Students who arrive from a British or Indian system frequently lose marks not on content but on criterion language: a Criterion D answer in Sciences asks for reflection on the impact of science, and a student who writes a good conclusion instead scores two. The personal project in Year 11 is a separate piece of assessed work with its own process journal.
programmes.countryNote: Middle Years students in Al Zahiyah are usually at a campus in Al Bateen, Al Nahyan or Al Reem Island, and they are the group most squeezed by the bus. A 16:45 online start on two weekdays, with the criterion rubric open on screen alongside the work, is the pattern that holds through the term for this age in this district.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The Diploma is six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Each subject carries an Internal Assessment worth roughly twenty to thirty per cent of the final grade, marked by the teacher and moderated externally. Subject grades run one to seven, with up to three further points available from the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay matrix. UAE schools sit the May session.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma students in Al Zahiyah face the longest day of anyone in the district: an early bus, a 15:00 finish, a long return, then coursework for six subjects. The families who cope best split tuition into two shorter weekday sessions plus one longer weekend block, because a single ninety-minute session at 18:00 on a Tuesday after that commute produces very little.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme pairs at least two Diploma courses with a career-related study, a reflective project, a service-learning component and a personal and professional skills course. It is offered by a small number of UAE schools and suits students who want Diploma-standard academic subjects alongside an applied qualification. The reflective project is assessed against its own criteria and is the component students most often underestimate.
programmes.countryNote: Very few Abu Dhabi campuses run the Career-related Programme, so an Al Zahiyah family exploring it is usually comparing it against a British sixth form at a nearby campus. Tutoring here concentrates on the two Diploma courses taken at level and on structuring the reflective project, which has no textbook to work from.

abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor-in-al-zahiyah.subjectsIntro: These are the Diploma and Middle Years subjects Abu Dhabi island families request most often. Each note says what the component actually tests and where marks are lost, because the difference between a 5 and a 7 in the IB is almost never a gap in knowledge of the topic list.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Paper 1 is sat without a calculator, which is where Standard Level students lose most of their marks: algebraic manipulation they would do correctly on a graphic display calculator falls apart by hand. Higher Level adds proof by induction, complex numbers and vector geometry. The exploration is marked on mathematical communication as heavily as on the mathematics itself.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Every paper permits a graphic display calculator, so the examinable skill is modelling and interpretation rather than manipulation. Students lose marks by giving a numerical answer without stating what it means in context, and by rounding before the final step. Higher Level adds matrices, graph theory and a substantial statistics strand that students from a British background have not met.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Higher Level Physics adds rigid-body mechanics, induction and a quantum strand on top of the Standard Level core. The reliable mark-loser is the extended-response question that asks for an explanation and receives a calculation. Uncertainty propagation in the internal assessment is the second: students collect good data and then treat error bars as decoration rather than argument.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and the energetics strand carry most of the Higher Level difficulty, and curly-arrow notation is marked strictly. Paper 1 is multiple choice with no calculator at Standard Level, so mole arithmetic has to be fast and clean. In the internal assessment, a vague research question is the single most common ceiling on the mark for the exploration.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The syllabus rewards precise command-term discipline: outline, explain, describe and evaluate each have a defined expectation, and answering the wrong one costs marks even when the biology is right. Statistics appear in the internal assessment more than students expect, and a repeated-measures design with no justification for the sample size caps the exploration criterion.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagrams are not illustrations; they are marked. An unlabelled axis or a missing shift arrow loses the diagram mark even where the written analysis is sound. Higher Level adds theory of the firm and a third paper of quantitative questions. The internal assessment is three commentaries on recent news articles, and choosing an article with no clear diagram is the usual mistake.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is a guided analysis of an unseen non-literary text, which means advertising, speeches, graphic novels and infographics as well as prose. The individual oral requires a global issue and two extracts, one literary and one non-literary, and students who choose a global issue too broad to support ten minutes of analysis lose marks in the structure criterion.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Marks are distributed across productive and receptive skills, and the writing task is assessed partly on conceptual understanding, meaning register, audience and purpose. Higher Level requires study of two literary works. Students who speak excellent conversational English frequently underperform here because they never learned to signal text type in writing.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: The syllabus uses a defined toolkit of business tools, and examiners expect them applied to the stimulus rather than described in the abstract. Higher Level adds an extension to each unit and a longer research-based internal assessment. Students lose marks by writing about a company they know well instead of the company in the case study.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The exhibition asks for three objects linked to one internal assessment prompt, and the essay responds to one of six prescribed titles. Both are marked on the quality of the knowledge argument, not on the elegance of the writing. The commonest failure is an essay that discusses the topic of the title instead of the knowledge question inside it.

abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor-in-al-zahiyah.regionsIntro: Al Zahiyah does not operate as an isolated district. The school run, the parents' commute and the weekend all cross into the areas below, and the tuition timetable has to work around all of it. These notes describe what each area actually adds to an Al Zahiyah family's week.

regions.name: Al Maryah Island
regions.note: A short causeway from Al Zahiyah and the workplace for a large share of its working parents. Pick-up after an Al Maryah workday rarely gets a parent home before 18:00, which is the single strongest argument for an online session that does not need an adult present to open a door.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Reached over the Al Reem bridges and home to several campuses Al Zahiyah children attend. The bridge traffic between 15:00 and 16:00 is what pushes the bus return towards 16:30 rather than 15:50.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: A twenty-minute drive from Al Zahiyah and the location of one of the emirate's best-known Diploma campuses. Saadiyat-bound buses leave Al Zahiyah earliest of all, which is why a Diploma student on that route is often the one who needs a weekend session rather than a weekday one.

regions.name: Al Bateen
regions.note: The western end of the island, with several long-established private campuses and a short enough run that children on those routes are home by 15:45. These are the Al Zahiyah families for whom a 16:15 start is genuinely workable.

regions.note: Al Zahiyah's western boundary and the district's main after-school outlet. Many families protect a 16:30 to 18:00 block for sport or the Corniche cycle path, which pushes tuition to a 19:00 slot on those evenings.

regions.note: Across the Sheikh Zayed Bridge and the single biggest cluster of Diploma campuses serving the island. An Al Zahiyah child at a Khalifa City campus has the longest round trip of anyone in this lane and realistically cannot start a session before 17:00.

sections.heading: What a parent in Al Zahiyah is actually asking for
paragraphs: The phrase typed into Google is "IB home tutor in Al Zahiyah", and the literal request is for someone to arrive at an apartment on the island and teach. That is a reasonable thing to want and a real market exists for it. It is worth being direct about what IB Gram does and does not sell before the page goes any further: Diploma and Middle Years tuition here is one-to-one over live video, and IB Gram does not arrange home visits anywhere in the UAE, because home visiting is a service offered only in India.

The reason that is not a consolation prize becomes obvious once you look at the two constraints an in-home arrangement has to satisfy at once. A tutor must know the subject at the level your child is sitting, and must be physically able to reach Al Zahiyah at the hour your child is free. Both constraints are tight. The second one shrinks the pool of people who satisfy the first to whoever happens to live on the island or can cross a bridge in rush hour, and then asks them to be free between roughly 17:30 and 19:30 on a weekday.

For English, general mathematics or Middle Years sciences, that pool is large enough. For Higher Level Chemistry, Mathematics Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, Economics Higher Level or Theory of Knowledge, it empties fast. Parents discover this by phoning three agencies and being offered the same generalist, or by being told a specialist is available on Thursdays at 20:00 only. The travel requirement, not the teaching requirement, is what produced that answer.

Removing the journey changes which question gets answered first. The subject and level are matched, and the time is then set to whatever the bus timetable leaves free, including 16:15 on a short-run day or a Saturday morning for a student commuting to Saadiyat. The rest of this page gives you the figures and the arithmetic to judge that trade for yourself rather than taking it on assertion.

sections.heading: The Al Zahiyah school run, hour by hour
paragraphs: No competitor page in this market publishes commute arithmetic, which is strange, because it is the thing that decides whether a session time is real or imaginary. The table below works from the campuses Al Zahiyah children actually attend, the published end of their teaching day, and the return leg in afternoon traffic. The final column is the earliest hour at which a session can start and still get useful work from a student who has been awake since six.

Two patterns come out of it. Island routes to Al Bateen and Al Reem give a child roughly forty-five minutes at home before a 16:15 start is reasonable. Mainland routes across the Sheikh Zayed Bridge do not, and for those students the honest answer is 17:00 on a weekday or a weekend block instead. A family that books a 16:30 session for a child on a Khalifa City route will spend the first twenty minutes watching them eat.

The second pattern concerns Thursday. The UAE school week runs Monday to Friday with a shorter Friday, and the afternoon of the last full teaching day is when accumulated homework is heaviest. Several Al Zahiyah families deliberately leave that afternoon clear and double up on a Saturday morning, which works well when the tutor's availability is not constrained by a driving route.

Treat the final column as a planning figure rather than a rule. Sports fixtures, Model United Nations weekends and a school's own revision sessions all move it. The point of publishing it is that you can test any tutoring offer against it: if a provider proposes 16:00 for a child on a Khalifa City bus, they have not thought about your week.

sections.heading: What the travel premium costs, and what it buys
paragraphs: Start with the part of the bill nobody itemises. The gap between an online rate and an in-home rate for the same tutor teaching the same syllabus is travel, and in Abu Dhabi it is worth between a third and a half of the hourly figure. Bestimate's 2026 rate table for the UAE puts in-home one-to-one visits at AED 180 to 350 an hour, with independent home tutors quoted up to AED 500. Qualified subject tutors working online sit at AED 150 to 300 on the same survey, with Unitors publishing IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB from AED 200, and TutorChase quoting AED 270 for specialist work.

At the bottom of the market, EdFlik advertises from AED 45 to 65 an hour and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52, which generally means a university student or a graduate working outside their degree subject. At the top, BartyED publishes AED 650 for named premium tutors. Monthly packages circulating in this market run around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits. Every one of those figures belongs to the provider named next to it; none of them is an IB Gram price, and IB Gram publishes no rate card on these pages.

What the premium buys, honestly stated, is a person in the room. For a young child who needs an adult physically redirecting their attention, that is worth paying for. For a Diploma student working through Paper 3 questions on a shared screen with annotation, it buys the commute and nothing else. The question an Al Zahiyah parent should ask is not which format is better in the abstract but what the extra AED 100 an hour is purchasing in their particular case, every week, for two years.

There is one further line in that arithmetic. An in-home tutor's travel time is also your scheduling constraint: the slot is theirs, not yours. Across a Diploma year that converts into cancelled sessions when traffic fails, when a parent is late back from Al Maryah, or when the student has a fixture. Those lost sessions do not appear on any rate card and they are the most expensive part of the arrangement.

sections.heading: Online one-to-one against an in-home visit, compared on the island
paragraphs: Comparison tables in this market usually compare a provider against an unnamed competitor. This one compares two delivery models on the dimensions that decide an Al Zahiyah family's week, and the in-home column is a fair description of the market rather than a straw man. There are rows where the in-home model genuinely wins, and they are marked as such.

The decisive row is tutor pool. An in-home arrangement selects from people who can reach Al Zahiyah at your hour. Online selects from everyone who teaches the subject at the level. For a Standard Level subject with a large teaching population that distinction may not change the outcome. For Higher Level Chemistry with an internal assessment due in six weeks it decides whether your child works with a chemist or with a general scientist.

The second decisive row is session integrity across a year. Online sessions survive a sandstorm, a bridge closure, a school trip to Al Ain and a family trip abroad. In-home sessions do not, and the ones that fall through tend to fall through in the weeks when they matter most, because that is when everybody's diary is fullest.

Where in-home wins is attention management for younger children and anything that needs physical apparatus in the room. If your child is eight and cannot be left with a screen, the honest recommendation is an in-home tutor from the Abu Dhabi market rather than an online session, and this page is not going to pretend otherwise.

sections.heading: Where Diploma marks actually go missing
paragraphs: Parents in Al Zahiyah tend to describe the problem as a subject: she is struggling with Chemistry. Diagnosing it as a subject produces generic tutoring. Nearly every stalled Diploma grade in this district resolves into one of four specific, nameable failures, and each has a different remedy and a different time cost.

The first is command-term discipline. The IB defines its command terms, and an answer that describes when the question said evaluate will not score the evaluation marks however accurate it is. This is the cheapest failure to fix and the one that moves a 5 towards a 6 fastest, because the knowledge is already there. Two or three sessions spent marking the student's own answers against the published criteria usually does it.

The second is internal assessment scope. Across subjects, the single most common ceiling is a research question too broad to answer in the word count. A Chemistry exploration asking whether temperature affects reaction rate has nowhere to go; one asking about a specific rate constant across a stated range does. A tutor cannot write any part of that work, and should not, but can teach a student how to narrow a question and then give feedback on the student's own draft.

The third is pace in Paper 1 under no-calculator conditions, which hits Mathematics Analysis and Approaches hardest. The fourth is Theory of Knowledge, where students write about the topic rather than the knowledge question. These last two are the slowest to shift and need a term of weekly work rather than a pre-exam block, which is why a family that starts in January for a May session is choosing from a narrower menu of fixable things than one that starts in September.

sections.heading: ADEK, inspection bands and what a school report actually tells you
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi private schools are overseen by the Department of Education and Knowledge, ADEK, which according to the UAE government portal supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Dubai's equivalent is the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, Sharjah has the Sharjah Private Education Authority, Ras Al Khaimah has its Department of Knowledge, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. ADEK is named by almost none of the tutoring sites competing for this search, which is a strange gap on pages written for Abu Dhabi parents.

What a published inspection rating does and does not tell an Al Zahiyah parent is worth being precise about. A rating is a judgement about a school as an institution across its whole provision. It is not a prediction for one child in one Higher Level subject, and a campus rated highly overall can still have a thin teaching bench in a particular Diploma option in a particular year. The useful questions are narrower: how many students took this subject at this level last year, who teaches it, and when does the school set its internal assessment deadlines.

The regulator point that matters most for tutoring is separate from inspection. Private tutoring in the UAE runs on a permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered at government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Anyone offering private tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule has been published, so no figure should be quoted to you.

One further Abu Dhabi rule is worth knowing before you ask a teacher at your child's own campus for private lessons. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff have been reported to prohibit paid private tutoring of students enrolled at the teacher's own school, and the MoHRE permit carries a code of conduct that also bars serving students affiliated with the permit holder's own school. Treat that as press-reported and check the current ADEK policy document before relying on it, but do not assume your child's class teacher can simply be hired in the evenings.

sections.heading: Academic honesty: the line a tutor must not cross on an Internal Assessment
paragraphs: This is the part of the market where an Al Zahiyah family is most exposed, and it deserves plain language. Work submitted for an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay or a Middle Years personal project must be the student's own. Providers exist in this region that sell finished Internal Assessments outright, at prices around AED 3,750. Buying one is not a shortcut with a small risk attached; it is malpractice under IB rules and the consequence falls on the student, not the seller.

What a tutor may properly do is substantial, and worth spelling out so you can tell the difference. A tutor can teach the underlying content so the student has something to say. A tutor can explain what each assessment criterion is asking for, in the IB's own words. A tutor can interrogate a research question until the student narrows it themselves. A tutor can read a draft the student has written and give feedback on where a criterion is not yet met. A tutor can teach referencing conventions, data presentation and uncertainty treatment as skills.

What a tutor must not do is also clear. No tutor should supply text that ends up in the submission, restructure a draft on the student's behalf, choose the research question for them, generate the data, or edit a piece to completion. IB Gram's tutors work inside that boundary, and a session that drifts towards the wrong side of it is a session you should stop. If a provider offers to handle the coursework for you, that offer is the warning.

There is a practical reason beyond the rules. A student who has had an Internal Assessment produced for them walks into the written papers without the understanding the process was supposed to build, and the papers are the larger share of the grade. The families who get the most out of tuition use it to make the student capable of the work, which is slower in February and considerably faster in May.

sections.heading: Ramadan, Gulf Standard Time and when sessions actually happen
paragraphs: A tuition plan that ignores the UAE calendar fails twice a year. School hours shorten during Ramadan, the household rhythm moves around Iftar, and concentration in the late afternoon is not what it is in November. Al Zahiyah families manage this in one of two ways: a short pre-Iftar session in the late afternoon for a younger child, or a post-Iftar slot around 21:00 for a Diploma student, which is frequently the most productive hour of that month. An online session moves to either without anyone renegotiating a driving route.

Gulf Standard Time matters more than it sounds. Every session on this page is set in UAE time, and the tutor works to it rather than to their own. That removes the recurring error where a family books what they think is a 17:00 session and discovers it was set in another zone. It also means a student travelling in the Eid or summer break can keep the same slot, which is how continuity survives the long UAE summer holiday.

The academic year brings its own fixed points. Mock windows, internal assessment deadlines set by the school rather than by the IB, and the school's own revision programme all compete for the same evenings. The sensible planning move is to get the school's deadline calendar in September and work backwards, rather than responding to each deadline as it arrives. UAE schools sit the May session for the Diploma; confirm every specific IB date with your school's Diploma coordinator or on ibo.org, because published secondary sources disagree with each other.

Finally, the summer. Abu Dhabi empties for much of it, and families who keep one session a week through July and August are the ones whose children do not spend September recovering ground. A short weekly slot from wherever the family happens to be is a modest commitment with a disproportionate effect on the first term back.

sections.heading: Starting from Al Zahiyah, and what happens when no specialist is free
paragraphs: Every other page in this market ends with a form. This one ends with the part providers leave out: coverage is finite, and some subject-level combinations are genuinely hard to staff at short notice. Publishing that is more useful than pretending otherwise, because it tells you how much lead time to allow and what to do when the answer is no.

The pattern is consistent. Mainstream Standard Level subjects and Middle Years work are quick to match. Higher Level sciences and Mathematics Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level take longer, especially in the weeks either side of an internal assessment deadline when demand concentrates. Smaller Diploma options, second-language subjects and Theory of Knowledge are the hardest, because the teaching population for them is small everywhere, not just in Abu Dhabi.

When nothing is available for a subject, you are told so rather than offered a near-miss. A generalist teaching Higher Level Chemistry does damage: the student loses weeks, confidence drops, and the mark does not move. The alternatives offered instead are a waiting slot with a date, a different tutor for a subject that is causing less trouble but can be lifted now, or a short diagnostic session to work out whether the problem is actually the subject at all.

The sequence for an Al Zahiyah family is short. Tell us the campus, the subjects and levels, the bus arrival time, and the next deadline on the school's calendar. A free trial lesson follows, with the student rather than with you, in the real slot you intend to keep. If the match is wrong you say so and it changes, and nothing is paid until you are satisfied the person in front of your child knows the syllabus they are teaching.

faqs.question: Can I get an IB home tutor in Al Zahiyah who comes to the apartment?
faqs.answer: An in-home market exists on Abu Dhabi island and its published rates run from about AED 180 to AED 500 an hour, travel included. IB Gram is not part of it: Diploma and Middle Years tuition for UAE families is delivered one-to-one over live video, and home visiting is a service offered only in India. The practical effect in Al Zahiyah is that the tutor is chosen for knowing your child's subject at your child's level rather than for living within a short drive, and the session time is set by your bus timetable instead of someone else's route.

faqs.question: What time can an IB session realistically start in Al Zahiyah on a school-bus day?
faqs.answer: It depends which bridge the bus crosses. Children at Al Bateen, Al Reem Island and Al Mushrif campuses are usually back in Al Zahiyah between 15:30 and 15:50, so a 16:15 or 16:30 start works. Children on Khalifa City, Al Raha or Saadiyat routes are rarely home before 16:10 to 16:20, and for them 17:00 is the honest earliest start. Yas Island routes land later still and most of those families move their main session to a weekend morning. Booking before those times produces a session spent eating rather than working.

faqs.question: Which IB schools do children living in Al Zahiyah usually attend?
faqs.answer: There is no large international campus inside Al Zahiyah, so families commute. Island destinations include Al Bateen Academy, Repton Abu Dhabi, Brighton College Abu Dhabi and Abu Dhabi International School. Across the bridge, the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor holds Raha International School, GEMS American Academy Abu Dhabi, Al Yasmina Academy and The British International School Abu Dhabi, while Cranleigh Abu Dhabi on Saadiyat draws a steady number of island families. Those schools are named as neighbourhood context only; IB Gram has no affiliation with any of them and claims no endorsement.

faqs.question: How much do IB tutors charge for Al Zahiyah families?
faqs.answer: Read it as a range by format rather than a single number. Bestimate's 2026 UAE table puts qualified online subject tutors at AED 150 to 300 an hour and in-home one-to-one visits at AED 180 to 350, with independent home tutors quoted up to AED 500. Unitors publishes IB tuition from AED 200, TutorChase quotes AED 270 for specialist work, and budget platforms advertise from AED 33 to 65. Those are each provider's own published figures. IB Gram does not publish a rate card on these pages; the rate is set at consultation after a free trial lesson.

faqs.question: Does the Al Zahiyah to mainland commute make online tuition the better choice?
faqs.answer: For a Diploma student, usually yes, and the reason is arithmetic rather than preference. A child on a Khalifa City route is out of the house for roughly ten hours. Adding a tutor who also has to drive pushes the session towards 17:30 or later and makes it hostage to bridge traffic. An online session starts the moment the student has eaten, survives a closed bridge, and can shift to a weekend morning in a heavy deadline week. For a younger child who needs an adult physically present to stay on task, an in-home tutor from the Abu Dhabi market remains the stronger option.

faqs.question: Does a tutor visiting our Al Zahiyah apartment need a permit to teach privately?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tutoring in the UAE runs on a work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no fine schedule has been published, so treat any specific amount you see quoted as unverified. Ask any tutor directly whether they hold the permit.

faqs.question: Can an IB tutor help my child with the Internal Assessment without crossing IB rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a boundary worth knowing precisely. A tutor can teach the content the exploration depends on, explain each assessment criterion in the IB's own terms, press the student to narrow a research question until it is answerable, read a draft the student has written and say which criterion is not yet met, and teach data presentation, uncertainty treatment and referencing. A tutor must not supply text for the submission, choose the question, generate the data, or edit the piece to completion. Providers in this region sell finished Internal Assessments outright; that is malpractice under IB rules and the student carries the consequence.

faqs.question: How many IB sessions a week do Al Zahiyah families usually start with?
faqs.answer: Most begin with two sessions a week in one subject, each forty-five to sixty minutes, rather than a single long session. After an Al Zahiyah school run a tired student gets very little from ninety unbroken minutes, and two shorter contacts also keep pace with the school's weekly content instead of chasing it. Families on the longest routes to Saadiyat or Yas often invert that and take one ninety-minute weekend block instead. Frequency then rises for a fixed period before mocks and the May session, and drops back afterwards rather than running at full intensity all year.

faqs.question: Can lessons move to post-Iftar timing during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for Diploma students that slot is often the most productive of the month. School hours shorten during Ramadan and late-afternoon concentration drops, so Al Zahiyah families typically choose one of two patterns: a short pre-Iftar session in the late afternoon for a younger child, or a session around 21:00 after Iftar for an older student. Because delivery is online, the change needs no renegotiation of anybody's driving route; the slot simply moves. Sessions return to the term-time pattern after Eid, and the same flexibility covers travel weeks and the long UAE summer break.

faqs.question: What happens if no tutor covers my child's IB Higher Level subject?
faqs.answer: You are told, rather than offered a near-miss. Mainstream Standard Level subjects and Middle Years work usually match within a week. Higher Level sciences and Higher Level Mathematics Analysis and Approaches can take one to two weeks, longer around internal assessment deadlines when demand concentrates. Theory of Knowledge supervision and smaller language options are narrower still and occasionally unavailable. The alternatives offered are a waiting slot with a named date, starting on a different subject that can be lifted now, or a single diagnostic session to establish whether the subject is really the problem.

faqs.question: Is there a trial lesson before we commit to IB tuition?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is free, with no card details taken first. The trial runs with the student rather than with a parent, and it is deliberately scheduled in the slot you intend to keep so you find out whether 16:30 actually works after that day's commute. Afterwards the tutor reports what they found, which is frequently more specific than the school's own feedback: a command-term habit, a gap three topics back, or an internal assessment question that cannot be answered as written. If the match is wrong, say so and it changes before any payment is made.

faqs.question: Which IB Diploma subjects do Al Zahiyah parents ask about most?
faqs.answer: Mathematics leads, split between Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation, and the no-calculator Paper 1 drives most of those requests. Chemistry and Physics at Higher Level come next, usually when an internal assessment deadline is close or an organic chemistry or electromagnetism topic has stalled. Economics is a steady third, often because diagram marks are being dropped rather than because the theory is weak. English A Language and Literature appears around the individual oral, and Theory of Knowledge requests cluster in the weeks before the essay deadline across all subjects.

faqs.question: Does ADEK regulate private tutors as well as private schools?
faqs.answer: No, and the distinction matters. According to the UAE government portal, the Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in Abu Dhabi, which covers your child's campus and its published inspection rating. Individual private tutors sit under a different instrument: the MoHRE private tuition work permit under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. Separately, ADEK's professional-ethics rules for school staff have been reported to bar paid private tutoring of students enrolled at the teacher's own school, so do not assume your child's class teacher can be hired privately.

faqs.question: My child sits the Diploma next session and we have eight weeks. Is it worth starting?
faqs.answer: Yes, but the menu of fixable things is shorter than it would have been in September, and it helps to be realistic about which. Command-term discipline, paper timing, and converting known content into mark-scheme answers all move inside eight weeks, because the knowledge is already present. Building a topic from nothing, or rescuing an internal assessment with a research question that cannot be answered, does not. The productive version of a short block works from the last mock paper question by question rather than from the start of the syllabus, which is also how to tell a serious plan from a generic one.

intro.heading: The home-tutoring question, answered properly
paragraphs: Families in Baniyas search for a home tutor because it is the obvious shape of the thing: somebody arrives, sits with the child at the table, teaches for an hour, leaves. It is a reasonable mental model and it is worth examining honestly rather than dismissing, because for some students it is genuinely the right format and for most Diploma students it is not the format that decides the grade.

Start with what it costs. Published in-home rates in this emirate run from AED 180 to 350 an hour in the Bestimate Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table and from AED 200 to 500 among independent home tutors, read in October 2026. A qualified subject tutor teaching online is published at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour on agency rate pages. The gap between those two bands is not a quality premium. It is a journey, and in Baniyas — a large mainland district some thirty kilometres from the island, laid out across eastern and western sectors with Mussafah and Al Shawamekh nearby — the journey is long and the afternoon traffic is unpredictable.

Then consider what the hour contains. A visiting tutor's hour is an hour of teaching. What decides a Diploma grade is largely what happens between hours: the student's own written work, produced, marked against the published criteria, and returned with the specific reason each mark was lost. That part of the service is independent of whether anybody drove anywhere, and it is the part the cheaper end of the market leaves out entirely. A family comparing a visiting tutor at AED 300 with an online specialist at AED 250 should be asking which one marks written work, not which one is in the room.

So the plain statement: IB Gram does not offer home visits in Baniyas or anywhere else in the UAE, because home visiting is a service we run only in India. Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. We think that is the better purchase for a Diploma household here, and the argument is above rather than asserted. There are students for whom it is the wrong answer — younger children, students who need physical supervision to stay on task, students for whom a screen is itself a barrier — and we would rather establish that in a free trial than in month three.

The rest of this page is the material a Baniyas family can actually use. The cost comparison in a table with its sources. What the address within Baniyas changes and what it does not. Where a household's limited hours should go across six Diploma subjects. The supervision roles split out, so that nobody is confused about who does what with an Extended Essay. The honest version of the home-versus-online decision. How to decide between tuition and a school change. A setup checklist for the first month. And the limits we work inside.

One note on figures throughout. Every AED band quoted here belongs to the market, is attributed to a named published source and was read in October 2026. None of it is IB Gram's price list, and no statistic appears on this page without a source and a date behind it.

Every subject carries internally assessed work marked against published criteria, so the year is a chain of deadlines as much as a run-up to examinations.
programmes.countryNote: For a Baniyas household the practical consequence is that hours have to be rationed across six subjects plus three core components, and most families ration them badly by spreading thinly. The subject-group table on this page is an attempt to make that rationing decision explicit rather than instinctive.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Criterion-referenced assessment across eight subject groups, graded one to eight against four criteria per subject. Students arrive in DP1 fluent in reflection and inquiry language, which serves them well in the internally assessed work and less well in the timed written papers.
programmes.countryNote: The pattern we see most often from this route is a student who writes thoughtfully and runs out of time. That is a procedural problem rather than a comprehension one, and it responds to timed practice far faster than to further teaching of content the student already understands.

programmes.name: Cambridge or Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Terminal written papers with minimal coursework, tiered by board. Students arrive in the Diploma with strong examination technique and no experience of a long independent piece of assessed work, which is why the exploration or investigation is the first thing to go wrong for them.
programmes.countryNote: Where a Baniyas student changes school between Year 11 and DP1 — common where local provision ends earlier — the handover of information between schools is imperfect. A marked IGCSE script in a parent's hand is often the only diagnostic record that travels with the child.

programmes.name: IB Career-related Programme
programmes.description: A smaller route combining Diploma courses with a career-related study and a core of its own, available at a limited number of schools. Where it is offered it suits students who want a vocational anchor alongside academic subjects rather than six academic subjects.
programmes.countryNote: Availability in Abu Dhabi is limited and varies year to year, so a family interested in it should ask schools directly rather than assume. ADEK's published inspection outcomes describe whole-school performance; programme availability is a separate question for the admissions office.

abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor-in-baniyas.subjectsIntro: Six Diploma subjects and three core components compete for the same household hours. These notes say where tuition tends to repay the money and where it tends not to, which is information a provider has no commercial incentive to give.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.levels: AA and AI, HL and SL
subjects.description: Consistently the highest-return Diploma subject for tuition, because the faults are specific and diagnosable and the exploration is twenty marks the student fully controls. Higher Level Paper 3 is the least practised component in the whole Diploma and worth a fifth of the grade.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Good return. Organic mechanisms and energetics carry the marks, and Paper 2 demands a style of reasoning that students rarely practise in writing. The scientific investigation is marked on design rather than on tidy results, which is a correctable misunderstanding.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Strong return where mathematics is the hidden obstacle, which it often is. A physics problem a student cannot begin is frequently an algebra problem, and a tutor who establishes that first avoids a term spent teaching the wrong subject.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Return depends entirely on method. Students who revise by reading plateau; students who write answers against published criteria improve. A tutor whose sessions are explanation rather than marked writing adds little here, however knowledgeable.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Good return, because the faults are structural: diagrams drawn imprecisely, evaluation missing, commentaries that summarise a published article rather than applying a theory to it. All three are correctable within a handful of sessions.

subjects.name: English A Language and Literature
subjects.description: High return where feedback is on the student's own writing and low return where lessons discuss technique in the abstract. The Individual Oral is a specific assessed task that students almost never rehearse under conditions.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Moderate return. The common fault is describing an organisation rather than answering the question asked about it, and the quantitative content catches students who chose the subject expecting to avoid numbers.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Disproportionately good return and almost nobody buys it. Ten marks for the essay and ten for the exhibition against published instruments, with word limits of sixteen hundred and nine hundred and fifty, and very little structured teaching on how the instrument is applied.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Thirty-four marks with critical thinking alone worth twelve, and a four thousand word ceiling beyond which nothing is marked. Best supported at the research question and first draft stages; support in the final week mostly rearranges an argument that is already fixed.

subjects.name: A second or third language
subjects.description: Variable, and dependent on specialist availability rather than on the subject. Where no specialist in a given language and level is available in the emirate we say so rather than filling the slot with a generalist speaker of it.

abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor-in-baniyas.regionsIntro: Baniyas sits among the mainland districts below, which share its distance from the island's longest-established Diploma provision. The island communities appear as the contrast case.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: The neighbouring mainland district, with its own schools and a comparable journey to the island. In-person Diploma specialists are scarce in both, and for the same structural reason.

regions.name: Al Shamkha
regions.note: Settled villa housing further east, around half an hour from the island on a clear afternoon run. Families here face the same travel loading on any visiting tutor's rate.

regions.name: Al Reef
regions.note: Townhouses on the Dubai-side corridor, closer to the Khalifa City schools. The shortest mainland journey of this group and still long enough to price a home visit upward.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: The principal mainland school cluster, where many Baniyas students' schools and internal deadlines actually sit. Twenty-five to forty minutes from the island in the afternoon.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: Villa community with an IB continuum school nearby, so students who stay through the whole programme start the Diploma deadline chain earlier than transfers do.

regions.name: Al Bateen
regions.note: The island contrast case. Shortest journeys in the emirate and long-established Diploma provision, and still no surplus of Higher Level specialists willing to travel anywhere.

schoolClusters.city: The mainland corridor
schoolClusters.note: Where most Baniyas students attend. Earlier finishes and longer journeys than the island, and the cluster whose internal deadline calendars govern a Diploma tuition plan here. Students we support attend schools in this cluster; no relationship with any of them is claimed.

schoolClusters.city: Abu Dhabi island and the islands beyond
schoolClusters.note: Where the emirate's oldest Diploma provision sits, and where some Baniyas families send a child despite the journey. The commute is the cost of that choice and it is paid in study hours rather than in fees.

abu-dhabi/ib-home-tutor-in-baniyas.modesIntro: Three arrangements, all delivered over live video. Each is defined by what it includes rather than by how long it lasts, because inclusion is what separates the products in this market.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one with marked written work
modes.description: One live video lesson a week with the same subject specialist, plus written work set with an instruction about what to show, returned marked against the published criteria. The marking is the part that moves the grade; the lesson directs it.
bullets: A written diagnosis in the first week naming the specific faults found
Work marked against published criteria rather than ticked
A review date with a measure attached rather than an impression

modes.title: Core component blocks
modes.description: Short runs of sessions on Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay or an internal assessment, timed to the school's published deadlines. Bounded, inexpensive relative to a term, and aimed at components most households never budget for despite the marks involved.

modes.title: Two-subject arrangement for an examination year
modes.description: Where two subjects are genuinely at risk in DP2, two specialists on different days so written work has room to happen between them. We cap at two in a term, because beyond that the student's own week becomes the limiting factor rather than the teaching.
bullets: A stated limit agreed in advance rather than open-ended addition

sections.heading: What a home tutor in Baniyas costs, and what the hour contains
paragraphs: The table sets the three formats side by side with published figures and their sources. The important column is the last one, because it names what is included beyond the hour, and that is where the real differences sit.

The travel component is worth isolating. Published in-home rates run from AED 180 to 350 an hour in survey data and from AED 200 to 500 among independent home tutors. Published online rates for a qualified subject tutor sit at roughly AED 150 to 300. On the same teaching quality, the difference is a journey — and from Baniyas it is a long one, so the loading sits toward the upper end of those ranges rather than the middle. A family paying it should at least know that is what they are buying.

The inclusion question cuts across all three formats and matters more than any of them. Ask any provider who marks written work between sessions and against what. A tutor who reviews work verbally in the lesson is providing a different and cheaper service than one who marks a script against the published criteria and returns it annotated. Both are legitimate; they are not the same thing and they should not be the same price.

On monthly figures, which are more useful for a household budget than hourly ones: the same survey estimates AED 240 to 600 a month for a weekly one-hour session at budget level, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist examination-year support. Packages advertised in this market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. All of these were read in October 2026 and none of them is our price list.

sections.heading: Baniyas East, Baniyas West, and what the address changes
paragraphs: Baniyas is not one place. It is a large mainland district organised into eastern and western sides with numbered sectors, built up over decades, with a mix of Emirati family housing, villa compounds and apartment blocks, and Mussafah's industrial and commercial area close by. Families on different sides of it have genuinely different journeys and genuinely different local options.

What the address changes is small and worth being honest about. Which school cluster is nearest. How long the morning run takes and, more importantly, how long the afternoon return takes. Whether a tuition centre in Mussafah or out towards Khalifa City is a plausible evening trip. And whether a visiting tutor will come at all, which in practice depends less on the sector than on the total distance from wherever that tutor lives.

What the address does not change is everything that determines a Diploma grade. The six subjects are the same subjects with the same criteria, the same word limits and the same examination structure. Higher Level Paper 3 is worth a fifth of the grade in Baniyas West and in Al Bateen. The exploration is twenty marks either way. The scarcity of Higher Level specialists is a feature of the emirate rather than of a sector, and no address inside Baniyas improves it.

So the honest summary for a family comparing their own sector with the next one over is that the comparison is not the useful one. The useful comparison is between formats and inclusion lists, which is the first table on this page, and between subjects competing for the same household hours, which is the next one. Those two decisions are worth more than any amount of thinking about geography, and they are available to every household in the district equally.

sections.heading: Six subjects, limited hours: where should the money go?
paragraphs: A Diploma student carries six subjects and three core components. A household typically has the budget for one or two subjects of real support. That mismatch is the central planning problem and most families resolve it by instinct — funding the subject the child complains about most — which is not the same as funding the subject where an hour returns the most marks.

The table offers a view by subject group. Two patterns run through it. First, subjects where the fault is procedural and diagnosable repay tuition better than subjects where the fault is diffuse, because a specific fault can be attacked and measured. Second, the core components repay tuition disproportionately and are almost never funded, because they do not feel like subjects and nobody is complaining about them at the dinner table.

Theory of Knowledge is the clearest example of that second pattern. Twenty marks across the essay and the exhibition, both marked against published instruments, both with strict word limits, and most students receive very little structured teaching on how the instrument is applied to what they have written. Three to five sessions aimed precisely at that often returns more per dirham than the same money added to a fourth subject, and virtually no household budgets for it.

The row worth reading twice is the last one. Where a student is already at the top of a subject's range, tuition in it is a poor purchase and we will say so. A provider that accepts every subject a parent offers is not helping them ration; it is billing them. The question to put to any provider is which subject they would not take, and the answer tells you how they make decisions.

sections.heading: Who does what: school supervisor, private tutor, student
paragraphs: Confusion about roles is the most common way a well-intentioned family drifts into an academic honesty problem. The Diploma assigns a supervisor at the school for the Extended Essay and for internally assessed work, and that person has a defined role with defined limits. A private tutor is outside that structure entirely, which makes their limits tighter rather than looser.

The school supervisor advises on the research question, meets the student at defined points, comments on a draft within the rules the organisation sets, and ultimately authenticates the work as the student's own. A private tutor does not authenticate anything, does not replace the supervisor and should never give advice that contradicts them. Where a tutor's view differs from the supervisor's, the supervisor is the one inside the structure and the one whose judgement governs.

What a private tutor legitimately adds is teaching and questioning. Explaining what each criterion rewards and how many marks it carries. Discussing whether a chosen topic can support genuine reflection or critical thinking at all, which is a mathematical or disciplinary judgement rather than an editorial one. Reading what the student has written and asking the questions that expose an unsupported claim. Marking practice work against published criteria. None of that produces text for submission.

What a private tutor must never do is write, redraft to completion, supply sentences, provide solutions for live assessed work or sit beside a student during an assessment. We decline those requests and explain why to the student directly at the first session. A provider in this market advertises completed Internal Assessments at AED 3,750; buying one is academic malpractice and the consequence falls on the student's whole entry, not on the seller. The table splits the three roles out so that there is nothing left to be vague about.
